items.title: NDC Campaign Council denies Obi rift over N6.5bn campaign funds
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) Presidential Campaign Council has dismissed reports of a disagreement between the party’s leadership and its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, over alleged withholding of N6.5 billion in campaign funds. The council described the reports as false and an attempt to create division between the party and its candidate ahead of the 2027 presidential election. In a statement signed on Monday by the Spokesperson of the NDC National Campaign Council, Dr Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, the council said Obi had neither complained about a shortage of campaign funds nor expressed dissatisfaction with the party’s handling of campaign financing. Ikokwu said the relationship between the party and its presidential candidate remained cordial, with both sides focused on winning the election and offering Nigerians an alternative. She argued that Obi’s campaign activities across the country demonstrated his commitment to the presidential contest, adding that the reports were intended to distract the party from its objectives. The statement read in part: “The reports circulating in sections of the media suggesting a disagreement or quarrel between the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and its presidential candidate, Mr Peter Obi, over campaign funding are completely false and should be dismissed for what they are: a deliberate attempt to manufacture friction where none exists. “Let me state categorically that Mr Peter Obi has not complained about a lack of campaign funds or expressed any dissatisfaction with the party over funding. “His commitment to reaching Nigerians across the country is there for all to see, and he’s doing that superbly. The campaign so far is a resounding success.” The council said the party’s leadership had responsibilities relating to the administration and management of its structures, adding that these should not be misconstrued as disagreements over campaign funding. It urged party members and supporters to avoid distractions, particularly with the election approaching. “Those attempting to engineer a needless quarrel should not mistake their wishful thinking for reality. We are united, focused and determined. Nigerians want a new direction, and nothing will distract us from taking that message to every corner of this country,” the statement added. However, allegations have emerged from some members of the NDC National Campaign Council that the party’s national leadership had not released sufficient funds for key campaign activities, including grassroots mobilisation, billboard advertisements and the printing of campaign posters. The members reportedly alleged that more than N6 billion was being held in a fixed account by the party’s national leadership while the campaign struggled to meet basic operational needs. They further claimed that the money was raised from aspirants who joined the NDC alongside Obi, with about 75 per cent allegedly contributed by aspirants from the South-East. The allegations have not been independently verified, while the campaign council has denied that Obi has expressed dissatisfaction with the party over funding. The council maintained that the party remained united and committed to its presidential campaign. items.title: The Right’s Absurd Misreading of Orwell
items.description: “Orwell Saw This Coming” ran the headline, and if you didn’t read any further, you might agree. The president was whipping up hatred in elaborate rage-fueled rallies and plastering banners bearing his glowering, oversize face on government buildings. The National Guard was patrolling the streets of Washington. Officials in the recently renamed Department of War were bragging about extrajudicial killings. The national-security apparatus had divided the world into three zones of influence, strikingly similar to The Party’s Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia from 1984 . But none of that was the this in “Orwell Saw This Coming,” which ran in The Free Press in January. This was New York City’s new mayor. “It’s fair to say that George Orwell would have despised Zohran Mamdani,” the columnist Charles Lane argued. Trump was hardly mentioned. In 2026, if an American writer brings up Orwell, chances are high that their target is the left, not the right. Over the past decade, one of the strangest habits among right-wing intellectuals and pundits has been their use of Orwell to defend the rise of authoritarianism in the U.S. The reference is shockingly common . “If 1984 has a practical lesson, it is this: There is a world of difference between a despotism dedicated to the expansion of socialism through federal-government power and a despotism dedicated to dismantling it,” Nathan Schlueter wrote in 2017 in National Review . “The former suffocates; the latter, though not without its serious dangers, just might create room to breathe.” The most direct rebuttal to this absurdity is Orwell’s own: “My recent novel is NOT intended as an attack on Socialism or on the British Labour Party (of which I am a supporter)” he once wrote to a curious reader. Orwell was literally antifa. In Spain, he fought with the militia of the Workers’ Party of Marxist Unification. Barcelona has a square named after him, and not because he supported far-right authoritarians against academics and students, as many conservative intellectuals would seem to believe. [ From the May 2024 issue: What Orwell really feared ] Let’s call them the Orwellian Trumpists. They could not have misunderstood the writer, or the current political reality, any more thoroughly. To a certain extent, Orwell saw this coming. The dumbest mistakes are typically made by the intelligentsia, he once cautioned: “No ordinary man could be such a fool.” He has now become the subject of his own warning. Orwell transcends right and left in this sense: Everyone who writes a political opinion in English, whatever their persuasion, is following in his tradition. “Why I Write” and “Politics and the English Language” are the foundational texts of magazine and newspaper writing to this day. His style is so hard to replicate because it is so basic. Reading Orwell is like hearing a man say what he means. It’s an astonishingly difficult effect to imitate. I’m trying to write like him now. Almost every opinion writer you can name is trying to write like him too. The roots of right-wing Orwell worship are not hard to see when you consider his obsession with prose style and the debasement of political language. Orwell believed in political writing more than any other writer; he gave it a grandeur and a sense of purpose that play to the vanities of every opinion columnist. He believed in clarity, not just freedom of speech. Staleness, imprecision, and pretension were, for him, far more than technical flaws. They were signs of the onset of dehumanization. Over the past decade, as the banalities of identity politics entered academia and journalism, Orwell became an ideal lens by which to witness and critique the process. The left’s attempt to impose a new linguistic order by force of shame was, in fact, an attempt to repress the human. But the problem with today’s right-wing Orwellians is that they are living in the past. Trumpism is a far greater threat to the values Orwell fought for than wokeness ever could be. “The Orwellian Big Brother punishing you for expressing an impolitic thought is now the law of the land in the land of Orwell,” Rupa Subramanya, another writer for The Free Press , told a congressional committee last year. She said this while the Republican Party was detaining students for signing op-eds, and policing the border by looking for inappropriate social-media posts. DOGE, meanwhile, was pulling funding from government agencies on the basis of keyword searches. Everyone who has ever argued that the most significant threat to the Western canon comes from the left will need to reckon with the fact that Republicans were the ones who told professors to pull passages from Plato from a course at Texas A&M. It was Republicans who threw CDC data sets and significant chunks of the National Archives into a memory hole. Trump’s decrees about language have gone further than any Democrat ever dared: He changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Lake Ontario, to his obedient followers, is Lake America. The Orwellian Trumpists’ claims to support linguistic freedom are laughable, or beside the point. In their bitter partisanship, they resemble the neoconservatives of a previous era, the liberals mugged by reality. They lack the dignity of their predecessors, though. They’ve been mugged by reality television. I think of them as the Otto intellectuals: Otto is the character from the 1980s British comedy A Fish Called Wanda who thinks that Aristotle was Belgian and that the central message of Buddhism is every man for himself. The contortions of the Orwellian Trumpists would dazzle any Soviet apparatchik. The British historian Niall Ferguson, who has used Orwell’s line that “to see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle” on multiple occasions, has frequently sane-washed Trump’s foreign policy. In an episode of the Hoover Institution’s podcast GoodFellows about Trump’s “coercive diplomacy,” Ferguson claimed that Trump’s destruction of America’s alliances and his sprawling, pointless violence were the result of deep strategic thinking. If you’re arguing in favor of “coercive diplomacy,” a phrase precisely as meaningful as “violent seduction,” you’re not George Orwell. You’re closer to Lord Haw Haw. Sometimes, as with the right-wing activist Christopher Rufo, using Orwell has explicitly partisan purposes. “What happens is that the left will say, ‘Well you’re opposing DEI; you don’t like diversity, you don’t like equity, you don’t like inclusion,’” Rufo said on his YouTube channel. “And you can say no, those are false words, those are Orwellian terms.” Citing Orwell becomes a technique in such cases, although aimed at a negligible slice of the political sphere: people who have heard the word Orwellian but have never bothered to think through what it means. [ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The right is changing the rules of the culture war ] As Orwell wrote in “Politics and the English Language,” he hated any argument that “consists in gumming together long strips of words which have already been set in order by someone else, and making the results presentable by sheer humbug.” Orwell has become what he most despised. He has set the strips of words in order, and someone else is gumming them together by sheer humbug. He’s jargon now. He’s the jargon for the supposedly anti-jargon crowd. Orwell’s contradictory status reminds me of his magnificent essay on Charles Dickens. Orwell is as distant from us today as Dickens was from Orwell. He was trying to understand how Dickens could be appropriated by people he would obviously have despised. “Dickens attacked English institutions with a ferocity that has never since been approached,” Orwell wrote. “Yet he managed to do it without making himself hated, and, more than this, the very people he attacked have swallowed him so completely that he has become a national institution himself.” The audience remembered his sentimentality. The actual import of his writing vanished. Dickens was critical of virtually every entrenched system in English life but even more critical of the attempts to overturn those systems. Tradition was brutality; revolution was terror. Dickens walked a line between “attacking everybody and antagonizing nobody,” Orwell wrote. In the end, Orwell could not suppress his adulation for the contradiction, for the refusal to fit: Dickens was “a type hated with equal hatred by all the smelly little orthodoxies which are now contending for our souls,” he wrote. Those orthodoxies, unable to face Dickens’s recognition of their own fraudulence but unable to reject him because of the power of his writing, turned him into a vibe. The Dickens vibe remains in place today: squalid London, Christmas, cheekiness, wretched children. Orwell is being turned into a vibe just as Dickens before him. He is English to the fingertips: late-imperial, pre-multicultural, pubs with barmaids who call you “dearie,” memorized passages of Kipling, bad food, warm beer, and floggings in public schools—combined with a staunch criticism of every bit of that. Orwell was an Eton graduate who nonetheless described the upper classes as drunken, violent buffoons who were tolerable only at the moment they were being shot. At the same time, he was a committed leftist who became a critic of the totalitarian left as it took power across various states in the middle of the 20th century. The Orwell vibe is “aren’t English people clever?” meets “internal critic of the left.” As with Dickens, the vibe is half correct, half oblivious. The reason Orwell is such a paragon—the reason you can still feel the power of his writing long after every politician he mentioned is dead—is that he remained a party of one, even when he was shooting people or elephants, even when highly civilized human beings were flying overhead , trying to kill him. Now he exists through his contradictions: an Englishman who saw the brutality of England and yet remained English, a leftist who faced the brutality of Communism and yet remained a leftist. “The words of a dead man are modified in the guts of the living,” as W. H. Auden said about Yeats. You can do what you like with Orwell’s words now. The Orwellian Trumpists have used their purported idol to justify a president who demands his followers accept obvious lies, who runs the government according to a standard of personal loyalty, who campaigns on two-minute hate, who revels in suspending the rules of war, who tears children from their mothers, who pardons for a fee, who has done everything in his power to separate language from meaning in order to camouflage his own brutality. They find themselves in an untenable position: Either they wanted all this or they have to admit that they got suckered by the most obvious con man in the history of con men. Perhaps it was inevitable that Orwell would devolve into just another vibe. But it’s shameful what that vibe turned out to be; the Orwellian Trumpists have chosen a boot stamping on a human face. It remains true that to see what’s in front of one’s nose requires a constant struggle.

items.title: How the Blue Wave Missed Florida
items.description: When the midterms’ blue wave hit the southern United States a few weeks ago, one conspicuous red patch remained: Florida. There, unlike in nearby Georgia and Texas, Democrats running for senator and governor both lost their races—narrowly, but still. Much of the explanation for Florida’s enduring redness is that the state has absorbed hundreds of thousands of newcomers in recent years, and these individuals largely moved to Florida in order to be Republican . Starting in 2020, Florida became a magnet for Republicans from other states who yearned for a place with conservative politics and a relatively low cost of living. Research shows that people who moved to the state from around the country during the past six years were much more likely to register as Republicans than Democrats. And this month, many of these new arrivals voted to support the Republican policies that they’d relocated to enjoy. As the Republican senator Ashley Moody said in her victory speech on Election Night, many of the newcomers she met during her campaign “were desperate to hold on to what we have built here in this state.” For many years, Florida was a quintessential battleground. Liberal retirees largely settled on the state’s east coast, in solidly blue Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach Counties, while conservative retirees flocked to the panhandle and parts of the Gulf Coast. The state’s Democrats and Republicans largely balanced each other out: George W. Bush eked out a victory in 2000 in part by the grace of hanging chads , then won handily in 2004. Barack Obama won the state in 2008 and 2012; in 2016, Donald Trump beat Hillary Clinton by just over 100,000 votes. In 2018 , Democrats outnumbered Republicans in Florida by more than 200,000 registered voters. [ Read: Why people won’t stop moving to the Sun Belt ] Then came COVID. Many blue states had mask mandates, vaccine mandates, and prolonged school closures. Several of them placed new restrictions on policing after George Floyd’s murder or required the teaching of LGBTQ issues in public-school classrooms. Governor Ron DeSantis seized the opportunity to advertise Florida as a warm refuge from the cold winds of wokeness. He offered police officers a financial reward if they moved there from another state. He proclaimed the rise of the “free state of Florida”—even adding the line to highway welcome signs . “Occasionally you come across a tagline that really sticks, and that one did,” Susan MacManus, a political scientist at the University of South Florida, told me. The state’s lack of vaccine mandates, its aggressive school-reopening approach, and restrictions on teaching about sexual orientation were popular with right-leaning parents. So were the lack of state income tax and the prospect of going to the beach in February. A recent study by Daniel Smith, a political scientist at the University of Florida, and his colleagues found that, starting in 2020, the people who moved to Florida were much more likely to register on arrival as Republican than Democrat. Smith found that registered Republicans overall have lived in Florida a shorter amount of time than Democrats, and Democrats and independents from the Northeast are coming to Florida in much smaller numbers than they used to. By the beginning of this year, Florida had about 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats. Republican candidates in Florida had other advantages in the midterms, too. Byron Donalds raised more than six times as much money for his gubernatorial campaign as his Democratic rival, David Jolly. And the state’s Hispanic population might have been especially receptive to attacks on Democrats. “Trump and then other Republicans really labeled the Democrats successfully as socialists,” Aubrey Jewett, a political scientist at the University of Central Florida, told me. That might have turned Cuban Floridians, many of whom had negative experiences with that country’s socialist government, away from any candidate even notionally associated with democratic socialism—such as Angie Nixon, Moody’s Democratic rival for the Senate. But experts I spoke with nevertheless said that migration from other states helped push Republicans over the top. Especially with remote work an option for large numbers of white-collar workers, Jewett said, “we have imported hundreds of thousands of Republicans over the last five years.” Paul Chabot, the CEO of GOP Agent, a real-estate company that connects people with conservative Realtors, told me that on top of good weather and a low cost of living, his clients “are looking at pro-gun-friendly states.” They don’t want to live in a state with “a George Soros–funded” district attorney, he added, “because they feel like they won’t be safe there.” So they come to Florida, where Governor-Elect Donalds has an A+ rating from the National Rifle Association and three-quarters of the state’s elected prosecutors are Republican. To understand the distinctiveness of this Republican influx, consider Florida alongside Texas, a historically red state that saw a blue wave in the midterms. Like Florida, Texas welcomed hundreds of thousands of migrants from other states from 2020 to 2026. But research has shown that newcomers to Texas were more evenly divided among Democrats, Republicans, and the unaffiliated, and have not affected the state’s partisan balance by much. The “majority of the people who are moving to Texas from other states are doing it for economic reasons or family reasons,” Mark P. Jones, a political scientist at Rice University, told me. [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Texas has seen some “political refugees” from California and other liberal states who do vote overwhelmingly Republican, Jones said. But left-leaning economic migrants seem to have arrived in larger numbers, and when many of them settled around Austin for tech jobs, they turned some of its surrounding counties blue, Jones said. In recent years, the state’s Republican politicians—three of whom had been in office for more than 10 years—were not popular, he added, and moderate Republican voters began to see Democrats as more palatable. Texas is still pink, Jones said—not quite purple. But, he said, “even a pink state can’t withstand an exceptionally unpopular president, a deeply flawed U.S. Senate candidate ,” and “a moribund economy that Republicans essentially hold all the responsibility for.” Whether Florida will continue on as a red state or shift back toward purple is unclear. Migration to the Sunshine State is slowing for a number of reasons. Some companies are calling remote workers back to the office, meaning that fewer people have the option to move wherever they wish. Plus, now that the COVID era is over, DeSantis is about to be out of office, and even some Democrats are disavowing the excesses of “ Woke 1 ,” the “free state of Florida” might not beckon the way it once did. Without a steady flow of conservative arrivals, the state could start tilting back to the center—or eventually to the left. People who were born in Florida are much less likely to be Republican than newcomers are, Smith said. And young voters, who are likelier to be Democrats, will eventually replace the state’s Baby Boomers as the latter go to that great beach house in the sky. Florida Democrats did notch some wins in the midterms: Pia Dandiya picked up a Florida House seat that “Republicans thought for sure they were going to win,” Smith said. Palm Beach County—home of Mar-a-Lago—went for both Jolly and Nixon in significant numbers. Many likely thought Texas was safely Republican too, until it wasn’t. Another definition of free , after all, is “up for grabs.”

items.title: An Ode to Executive Assistants
items.description: T he executive assistants are being laid off. According to Bloomberg , firms such as PwC and McKinsey have cut thousands of assistant and other support-staff positions. From the start of 2023 until the summer of 2025, openings for entry-level jobs typically requiring at least some college dropped by 35 percent . What executive needs a 23-year-old with student loans and big dreams when they can use a personal AI assistant to manage their calendars and book their flights for free? You might think that this position is a perfect candidate for robot replacement. If AI can do mindless administrative tasks as well as any human, then all that’s left is the emotional labor, which can be heavy—managing the hyperspecific preferences and enormous egos of entitled corporate titans. Get rid of this position, and businesses would save money while young people would—perhaps—find less humiliating jobs. But I spent almost two years as an executive assistant, and one of the many things I learned was that no one—not even the bosses who might want to replace us—had any sense of what we actually did. These positions play an important role in the job market, providing a rare entry point into competitive fields. Executive assistants run last-minute errands. They steer their bosses away from annoying people at dinner parties and memorize faces and relationship histories. They know their boss’s intimate secrets and how to anticipate their needs. They put out fires before the boss smells smoke. They serve as office managers, nannies, baristas, and human encyclopedias. The better an assistant is at their job, in other words, the less anyone knows what they do all day. And when they’re gone, we’re really going to miss them. I f you ask executive assistants what they think about being replaced by AI, they might say that they welcome a robot taking over chores like filing expenses, but that they can’t imagine handing over the trickier parts of their job. Maguire Grace Amundsen was Kylie Jenner’s executive assistant for more than two years. She’s now a sort of girlboss influencer, and is starting an interview series with high-powered women called Hot Commodities . Being a good executive assistant, she told me, requires understanding “a lot that is not said.” You have to know “the person that you’re working for in a way where even if they don’t say something, you kind of know what they’re saying.” You have to understand their every mood. One woman, who used to be an executive assistant to a famous fashion designer and his chief marketing officer, and asked to remain anonymous because she had signed an NDA, said that if the designer “was in a good mood, it’s fine to send the email asking if it’s okay that the car is not a Range Rover for Friday. But if he’s in a terrible mood, sending that is literally going to kill your day.” “AI can’t predict all that,” she told me. Companies would need to “hire a human assistant to handle the AI assistant.” [ Sophie Gilbert: The Assistant and the messes women clean up ] Samantha, another former executive assistant, who asked me to use only her first name because she also signed an NDA, said that one of her most important roles was to serve as the scapegoat when anything went awry. She worked in the finance industry, and said a lot of her job was “taking the sword, and not taking that personally.” If something goes wrong anywhere in the company, you may be the one your boss yells at, and you get used to taking ownership for mistakes that weren’t your own. Samantha said she was privy to some of “the most intimate and personal things” in her bosses’ life: “colonoscopies, bonus sizes, who’s getting fired, who’s getting promoted, is divorce on the table.” The fashion assistant told me that the CMO’s “husband would call me. I talked to her driver. I talked to her hair stylist. I talked to her facialist. I talked to her kids. I talked to their school teachers.” At a time when most Americans distrust AI , it’s hard to imagine high-profile individuals wanting to share this kind of private information with a bot. But the more an executive assistant knows their boss, the more proactive they can be. High-powered executives often don’t have time to give instructions, and their assistants have to make judgment calls. “AI is really great at doing what you tell it to do, but a really good executive assistant is constantly thinking 345 steps ahead,” Samantha told me. “An EA needs to have the capacity to handle situations that don’t come with a clear set of instructions, whereas AI will always need a clear set of instructions.” Even if an executive theoretically fed an AI chatbot every bit of information (a big ask for someone who hires someone else to send their emails), there’s a level of nuance and emotional intelligence that you don’t get unless you are physically present in the room. Plus, most executives are looking to spend less time on their devices, not more. One of the main things assistants do is figure out what their boss actually needs to know from the onslaught of digital notifications and noise. “If you’re good at your job, you do a really great job of filtering, and I think that element would be lost,” Amundsen told me. To be fair, if you ask most anyone in most any field whether they think they can be replaced by AI, they’re likely to say absolutely not . But executive assistants have one more thing going for them: Perhaps the biggest reason executives like having them around is simply to flaunt them. “There is a level of prestige to having a dedicated assistant,” Anthony Taylor, an executive assistant at Hermès, told me. It’s how you know you’ve succeeded. He used to work at a smaller agency, where his old boss would bring him to events just to show that she was important enough to bring him to events. It’s the same reason that people send emails “looping my assistant in.” [ Annie Lowrey: How ChatGPT will destabilize white-collar work ] “No one’s going to be impressed by the fact that you’re paying some subsidiary of Claude to manage your calendar and your emails,” Taylor said. For this reason, human assistants will probably continue to have a place in status-obsessed industries that want to signal their refined taste, if nowhere else. These assistants don’t just book cars; they make sure the driver is wearing the right outfit and carrying the right brand of mints. They don’t just book the restaurant; they book the impossible restaurant, the kind you can’t get into unless someone at the hospitality group that owns the whole establishment owes you a favor. They cultivate their own network of maître d’s and publicists, and when their boss brings them to an event, they’re a status symbol in flesh and blood. T ake away the assistants , and lots of executives would probably have meltdowns. But that’s not what worries me most. The position of executive assistant is especially valuable for young people with backgrounds like mine. I would probably not be writing for this magazine if I hadn’t landed a job as an executive assistant here in 2023. I came from the South, had no connections in journalism, and little experience in the field. What I did have was a master’s degree, a résumé full of odd jobs, and the willingness to take notes in meetings. Eventually, I elbowed my way off the business side of the magazine and into writing. My story is a common one for people who want to land jobs in competitive, creative industries, but don’t have the perfect résumé or connections. “I was very unequipped, network-wise, moving to the city and pursuing fashion in any capacity, especially fashion PR, which is notoriously insular and elitist,” Taylor, who was raised in Mississippi, told me. When Taylor, who’s now 25, first set out to move to New York, he scoured the internet for anyone who could help him get his foot in the door. “My first actual successful attempt at networking was I strategically went on a date with someone who I knew worked in the industry,” he told me. It worked—his résumé was sent to a few agencies. He got an unpaid internship for a few months, during which he “spent all of my savings trying to stay afloat.” Eventually, a communications-assistant position that involved working on brand accounts opened up. He applied, but the role was given to the daughter of an executive at a major fashion magazine. The executive-assistant job was his “consolation prize,” he said. It required humility, but it was his ticket into the industry. Some people say that everyone should have to work a service-industry job, because there are certain life lessons that can only be learned as a 19-year-old bussing tables for snobby customers. My version of this argument is that everyone in corporate America should have to work as an assistant in their industry for a year. There are few jobs as frustrating and formative. You will learn to earn your keep. And if you’re as lucky as I was, you gain generous mentors who have successfully navigated the industry you want to be a part of. [ Matteo Wong & Charlie Warzel: AI agents are here. Nobody’s ready. ] You learn resilience: to take blame when no fault is your own, to humble yourself, to take menial tasks seriously, to go overlooked and unthanked. You learn to make judgment calls and not need external validation to know you’ve done a good job. But most of all, being an executive assistant makes you learn people , which is the most valuable skill in almost any industry. Young people need proof that there’s still a ladder left to climb in corporate America, and that if they’re willing to start on the lowest rung, swallow their pride, and be someone’s executive assistant, they can make it to the top. So, long live the human executive assistant. May their days be plenty and may their bosses be pleased with them. And if the bosses can’t be pleased, let them have the satisfaction of yelling at a 20-something, instead of a screen.

items.title: La Guinée s’inspire de l’expérience du PUDC sénégalais
items.description: Une délégation gouvernementale guinéenne a séjourné au Sénégal, du 16 au 21 novembre 2026, pour s'imprégner de l'expérience du Programme d'urgence de développement communautaire (PUDC), notamment en matière de financement, de réalisation d'infrastructures et de suivi-évaluation. Le modèle sénégalais du développement communautaire suscite l'intérêt de plusieurs pays africains. Dernière illustration : une délégation gouvernementale guinéenne, conduite par l'ambassadeur Kabélé Soumah, Secrétaire général du ministère du Plan et de la Coopération internationale, a effectué une mission d'échanges au Sénégal avec l'appui du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD). Reçue le 17 novembre au siège du PUDC par son Coordonnateur national, Gade Kounta, la délégation a été édifiée sur le cadre institutionnel, les mécanismes de financement et les résultats du Programme. Celui-ci ambitionne de « faire en sorte qu'aucun Sénégalais ne soit laissé en marge du développement du fait de son lieu de résidence », a rappelé son coordonnateur. En un peu plus de dix ans, le PUDC a notamment réalisé plus de 1 090 kilomètres de pistes, électrifié plus de 1 170 villages, amélioré l'accès à l'eau potable dans plus de 2 050 villages et déployé plus de 5 800 équipements post-récolte. Des réalisations qui inspirent plusieurs pays africains, dont le Togo, la RDC, le Tchad, le Cameroun et la Gambie. Les 18 et 19 novembre, la délégation a effectué des visites de terrain dans les départements de Foundiougne et de Fatick. À Kébé Ansou et Keur Bakari Cissé, elle a découvert des infrastructures d'électrification bénéficiant à environ 1 765 habitants. À Sokone, une plateforme de transformation agroalimentaire traite jusqu'à 600 tonnes de noix de cajou au profit de 39 GIE. La mission a également permis de constater l'impact de la piste Passy-Thioyène, qui désenclave 36 villages et dessert plus de 22 000 habitants. À Ouyal Sandé, les visiteurs ont rencontré les 98 femmes du groupement Dialki Diék, qui assurent depuis 2019 la gestion de leurs équipements post-récolte. Grâce à leur organisation, elles ont constitué une épargne de 738 960 FCFA et acquis une broyeuse d'arachide sur fonds propres. La tournée s'est achevée au poste de santé de Ndiob, qui dessert 12 082 personnes dans 23 localités. La mission s'est poursuivie, le 20 novembre, au ministère des Finances et du Budget, autour des mécanismes de financement et du montage des projets, puis à l'Agence nationale de l'aménagement du territoire (ANAT). Au terme des échanges, plusieurs enseignements ont été retenus : le ciblage participatif des bénéficiaires, l'implication des communautés dans la gestion des ouvrages, la complémentarité des infrastructures et le rôle central de l'État dans la mobilisation des financements. Le Coordonnateur national du PUDC a toutefois insisté sur la nécessité d'adapter le modèle aux réalités de chaque pays, précisant que le programme « n'a pas vocation à être reproduit de manière uniforme ». Le Sénégal a ainsi réaffirmé sa disponibilité à accompagner la Guinée dans la conception et la mise en œuvre de son programme de développement local, en perspective notamment de ses ambitions dans le cadre de Simandou 2040.

items.title: 2027: Wabara urges opposition leaders to back consensus candidate
items.description: By Steve Oko, Regional Editor, South-East Former Senate President and Chairman of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) Board of Trustees, Senator Adolphus Wabara, has backed moves by opposition parties to present a consensus presidential candidate for the 2027 general elections, urging political leaders to sacrifice personal ambitions in the interest of rescuing Nigeria. Wabara said opposition unity had become imperative in view of the country’s political and economic challenges, insisting that national survival, democratic stability and the welfare of Nigerians should take precedence over individual presidential ambitions. The former Senate President, who spoke exclusively with Vanguard, urged opposition presidential hopefuls to rise above personal interests, ego and political calculations and rally behind a credible candidate capable of challenging the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). He said the moment demanded political courage, compromise and patriotism, warning that failure by opposition leaders to unite could weaken the country’s democratic space and prolong the hardship facing citizens. His position comes amid ongoing consultations among opposition parties, including the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Allied People’s Movement (APM) and Social Democratic Party (SDP), to forge a common front ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The parties are expected to deepen discussions at a proposed opposition summit scheduled for November 30, where the question of a consensus presidential candidate and a broader framework for political collaboration are expected to feature prominently. Wabara argued that the opposition’s strength lay not in the number of presidential candidates contesting against one another but in its ability to unite behind one candidate with the political capacity, national reach and popular support to challenge the APC. He warned that allowing multiple opposition candidates to divide the votes of Nigerians seeking change could give the ruling party an electoral advantage without a meaningful challenge. According to him, the overriding objective should be to rescue Nigeria from the control of a few political interests while millions of citizens grapple with economic hardship, insecurity, unemployment and declining living standards. Describing the country’s situation as a threat to democracy, Wabara called on opposition leaders to demonstrate statesmanship by supporting whoever emerges as the consensus candidate, even if doing so requires them to shelve their presidential ambitions. He said: “Nigeria is currently under captivity by a few cabal who should have no business being in power. Our democracy is at stake, and now is the time for uncommon sacrifices for our national survival. “I want the progressive opposition presidential flag bearers to put Nigeria above their individual interests. Let them present the best among them while others step down and rally support for the consensus candidate. Let’s rescue Nigeria first.” Wabara said the task ahead was not merely about winning an election or dislodging the APC but also about restoring democratic accountability, strengthening public institutions and giving Nigerians renewed hope in governance. He also expressed concern over the threats posed by electoral violence, vote-buying, rigging, voter intimidation and manipulation of electoral processes, urging opposition parties and citizens to unite in defending the integrity of the 2027 elections. He maintained that the ballot must remain the ultimate instrument through which Nigerians determine who governs them, warning against attempts to undermine the people’s mandate through violence, coercion or electoral manipulation. The former Senate President specifically urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to address shortcomings observed in previous elections, particularly the technical glitches that generated controversy during the 2023 presidential election. He also called on the electoral commission, security agencies and the judiciary to discharge their responsibilities impartially, warning that any action capable of eroding public confidence in their neutrality could undermine the credibility of the forthcoming elections. Wabara urged Nigerians not to succumb to political intimidation or voter apathy but to mobilise peacefully, protect their votes and demand credible elections. He reminded the ruling party that incumbency did not guarantee electoral victory, citing the defeat of the PDP in the 2015 general election as evidence that an incumbent ruling party could be voted out through the ballot. He said the transition demonstrated that Nigerians could change their government through democratic means when they united around a common purpose, adding that no political party had a permanent claim to power. Citing the recent United States midterm elections, Wabara argued that electoral outcomes could change even under an incumbent administration, declaring that the APC was not unbeatable. “The APC is defeatable even with the power of incumbency,” he said. He described opposition unity as the APC’s greatest political nightmare, arguing that a fragmented opposition often gives incumbents an advantage, while a united front could fundamentally alter the political equation. Wabara urged opposition parties to put aside mutual suspicions, internal rivalries and disagreements over political interests and concentrate on building a formidable alliance capable of inspiring confidence among Nigerians. He described the 2027 election as a defining moment for the country, warning that Nigeria could not afford another opportunity lost to political ego, division or the inability of opposition leaders to reach a common understanding. He also called on political leaders, civil society organisations, youths, labour groups and Nigerians across political divides to support the defence of democracy and demand peaceful, free, fair and credible elections. Wabara maintained that a united opposition, backed by Nigerians’ determination to exercise their democratic rights, could change the country’s political direction, insisting that the power to determine Nigeria’s future ultimately belonged to the electorate. The post 2027: Wabara urges opposition leaders to back consensus candidate appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: MTN donates computers to UMaT as student population grows
items.description: The University of Mines and Technology (UMaT), Tarkwa, is seeking to improve access to computer facilities after admitting more than 5,000 new students this academic year. Vice Chancellor, Professor Bernard Kumi-Boateng, said the increase in enrolment had put pressure on the University’s ICT resources, making it difficult to provide adequate computer access for all students. He was speaking at a presentation of computers and ICT accessories by MTN Ghana to the University as part of the telecommunications company’s 30th anniversary Acts of Kindness initiative. Professor Kumi-Boateng described the donation as timely, saying the equipment would support teaching, learning and research while improving students’ access to essential digital tools. He also commended MTN Ghana for its longstanding partnership with UMaT and its continued investment in education and technology. Acting Senior Manager for MTN’s South West Region, David Woasey, said the donation formed part of the company’s Computers-4-Social-Good programme, which provides educational technology resources to selected institutions across the country. He said digital skills were increasingly important in sectors such as mining, engineering, data science, cybersecurity and telecommunications, making access to technology essential for students. Mr Woasey said MTN hoped the computers would strengthen UMaT’s learning environment and help prepare students to contribute to Ghana’s digital and industrial development. The donation forms part of MTN Ghana’s 30th anniversary Acts of Kindness activities and its broader commitment to education and digital inclusion.

items.title: Endeavour Mining commits XOF 803m to health projects in three African countries
items.description: Endeavour Mining has committed XOF 803 million to support health initiatives in Ghana’s neighbouring countries, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso and Senegal, in 2027. The commitment was announced at the third edition of Speak Up Africa Day in Dakar, Senegal, where more than 400 stakeholders from government, business, science, civil society and the development sector gathered to discuss Africa’s health, education and inclusion priorities. The investment is expected to contribute to health interventions in the three countries, although details of how the funds will be distributed and the specific projects to be supported were not disclosed. The announcement came during a high-level engagement on the role of the private sector in malaria elimination and improving access to healthcare, particularly in communities where health needs remain greatest. Speak Up Africa, the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene, and OSIDEA used the gathering to encourage businesses, especially those in the extractive industry, to make sustainable investments in public health. The event also saw the launch of the Private Sector Health Investment Barometer, a tool intended to document corporate contributions to healthcare and encourage more businesses to support national health priorities. Four companies, Canal+, ICons, Boto S.A. and Endeavour Mining, were recognised for their contributions to the fight against malaria. Elhadji Doucoure, Head of Monitoring, Evaluation, Surveillance and Digital Transformation at Senegal’s National Malaria Control Programme, said private-sector involvement must translate into tangible investments that protect vulnerable communities. “The private sector has an essential role to play in malaria elimination. The challenge is to translate this engagement into decisive investments that support national strategies and protect communities where needs are greatest,” he said. Beyond malaria, the event highlighted the need to protect African children against preventable diseases. Speak Up Africa, in partnership with the Basketball Africa League (BAL), launched the First Shot campaign on November 14 in Guédiawaye, Senegal, to strengthen public and political support for child health. The campaign seeks to promote routine immunisation, malaria prevention and polio eradication, using sporting events and influential personalities to raise awareness. It is expected to run until the end of 2027. Former NBA player Ian Mahinmi, founder of the I AM Foundation, was among the personalities who supported the launch. Marie Laurence Archambault, Director of Social Responsibility and Player Programs at the Basketball Africa League and NBA Africa, said millions of African children still lack essential protection against preventable diseases. She said the partnership would use the influence of sport and its personalities to make child health a priority both within communities and at the policy level. Education was also a major part of this year’s gathering, with the launch of the Make It Count campaign, which advocates for every African child to acquire basic reading, writing and mathematics skills by the age of ten. The campaign is being led by Speak Up Africa and its partners through the Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Hub. In Senegal, the Harmonised Model of Bilingual Education (MOHEBS) has reached more than 640,000 students and supported 12,116 teachers across the country’s 18 education academies. Fara Ndiaye, Co-Founder and Deputy Executive Director of Speak Up Africa, said governments must translate their commitments to foundational learning into adequate funding and measurable results in classrooms. The programme also highlighted the contributions of women and young people to Africa’s development. An intergenerational gathering brought together women leaders from different sectors to share experiences and strengthen networks, while Story Lab Next Gen created a platform for young people, advocates and content creators to explore new approaches to public advocacy. Discussions also addressed reproductive health and family planning, with an emphasis on youth participation and access to essential information and services. The 2026 edition, which marked 15 years of Speak Up Africa, ended on November 20 with two exhibitions celebrating individuals working to advance health, education and inclusion. The exhibitions, titled “Jambaar” and “Leurs voix, nos regards”, featured portraits of African sports personalities and women whose work is contributing to health and women’s rights in their communities.

items.title: Mahama mourns former South African Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has paid tribute to former South African Deputy President Dr Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka following her death, describing her as an influential African leader whose contributions to gender equality, peace and security will be greatly missed. In a Facebook post on Monday, November 23, President Mahama extended his condolences to her family, the South African government and its people, highlighting her distinguished record in public service and her contributions to the continent and the international community. He recalled Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka’s service as South Africa’s Deputy President and her subsequent leadership of UN Women as Executive Director, where she played a prominent role in championing gender equality and advancing the rights of women worldwide. “Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka was a trailblazer whose impact resonated worldwide,” President Mahama wrote. The President also reflected on their professional association through the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa, which he chairs and where the former Deputy President served as a board member. He said the forum had benefited from her knowledge and experience, particularly her commitment to addressing issues of peace, security and development across the continent. “Her Excellency’s unwavering commitment to peace, security, and the development of our continent leaves a void that will be deeply felt,” he stated. Dr Mlambo-Ngcuka’s work at UN Women earned her international recognition for her advocacy for gender equality and efforts to advance opportunities for women and girls. Her contributions to both South African politics and international development made her a prominent voice in discussions on women’s empowerment and Africa’s progress. President Mahama concluded his tribute with a message of sympathy to her family and the people of South Africa, praying for her peaceful repose.

items.title: Fire destroys offices of Northern Regional Minister and Chief Director in Tamale
items.description: Fire has gutted parts of the Northern Regional Coordinating Council (NRCC) in Tamale, including the offices of the Northern Regional Minister and the Chief Director. The fire reportedly broke out at about 5:30 a.m. today, destroying computers, office furniture, equipment and important documents. The Chief Director’s office was the worst affected, with no single item reportedly salvaged from the inferno. The Chief Director is a key administrative figure at the RCC, overseeing its day-to-day operations and coordinating the activities of the various departments. It took the timely intervention of personnel from the Ghana National Fire Service (GNFS) to bring the fire under control and prevent it from spreading to other parts of the facility. However, no casualties were recorded. Briefing journalists after the incident, the Northern Regional Minister, Ali Adolf John, said he received information about the fire early in the morning. He noted that the incident had virtually grounded the operations of the RCC, considering the extent of the damage to offices and the destruction of essential equipment and documents. The Minister said preliminary investigations suggested that the fire could have been caused by an electrical fault. He added that the GNFS had commenced investigations to establish the actual cause of the fire.

items.title: CONTRIBUTION – KÉDOUGOU : DE LA RICHESSE MINIÈRE À LA PROSPÉRITÉ PARTAGÉE
items.description: Comment expliquer qu'une région disposant d'importantes ressources minières, agricoles et environnementales continue d'afficher un taux de pauvreté estimé à 67 % ? Ce paradoxe dépasse la seule question de la redistribution des revenus miniers. Il révèle les limites de la gouvernance économique, de la programmation des investissements publics et de la capacité des institutions à transformer les richesses produites en progrès social et économique. Située au sud-est du Sénégal, Kédougou compte environ 200 000 habitants et possède un patrimoine naturel considérable, notamment aurifère, ainsi que d'importantes potentialités agricoles, pastorales et environnementales. Pourtant, cette abondance contraste avec la persistance de difficultés sociales majeures. La véritable question n'est donc pas seulement de déterminer quelle part des revenus miniers doit revenir aux populations, mais comment organiser l'économie territoriale pour que ces richesses génèrent durablement des emplois, des infrastructures, des services sociaux et des activités productives. Kédougou constitue l'une des principales zones aurifères du Sénégal. L'exploitation industrielle et artisanale de l'or y mobilise des investissements importants et attire de nombreux travailleurs. Les estimations évoquent près de 32 000 personnes engagées dans l'orpaillage. Par ailleurs, les données mentionnées dans le rapport ITIE 2024 font état d'une contribution financière du secteur extractif pouvant atteindre 400,55 milliards de FCFA, dont le périmètre national et la ventilation territoriale méritent d'être précisés. Cependant, la production de richesses ne garantit pas leur transformation en développement local. Le recours aux fournisseurs extérieurs, l'importation des équipements et la faible circulation des revenus dans l'économie régionale limitent les effets d'entraînement sur les autres secteurs. L'enjeu consiste ainsi à passer d'une économie d'extraction à une économie de création et de circulation de valeur ajoutée, en renforçant les relations entre entreprises minières, PME locales, producteurs, artisans et établissements de formation.Les besoins des entreprises minières en transport, restauration, maintenance, construction, logistique et prestations techniques représentent autant d'opportunités pour les entreprises locales. Une politique ambitieuse de contenu local devrait reposer sur un programme régional de développement des PME et de sous-traitance locale, assorti d'objectifs progressifs de commandes ; un dispositif d'accompagnement technique et financier des entreprises locales ; une plateforme de mise en relation entre sociétés minières, fournisseurs et organisations professionnelles ; des mécanismes de crédit, de garantie et de facilitation de l'accès aux marchés ; des partenariats avec les établissements de formation professionnelle pour adapter les qualifications aux besoins des entreprises. Cette politique doit intégrer des engagements mesurables en matière d’emploi des jeunes et des femmes, de formation et d'insertion professionnelle. La performance d'une mine devrait également être appréciée à l'aune de sa contribution à la construction d'un tissu économique local compétitif. Instituer un mécanisme territorial de financement du développement La redistribution des revenus miniers ne suffit pas sans une programmation stratégique des investissements. Il serait pertinent de créer un Fonds territorial de développement et de transformation économique de Kédougou, articulé aux dispositifs légaux existants et associant l'État, les collectivités territoriales, les travailleurs, les entreprises et les communautés riveraines. Son financement pourrait combiner ressources légalement affectées, dotations publiques, contributions conventionnelles des entreprises et partenariats au développement. Sa gouvernance devrait garantir une affectation transparente des ressources, une programmation pluriannuelle privilégiant les infrastructures structurantes (eau, routes, électrification, santé, éducation, formation et équipements économiques), une participation effective des populations et des collectivités aux choix et au suivi des investissements, ainsi qu’un contrôle indépendant couronné par la publication annuelle des ressources mobilisées, des projets financés et des résultats obtenus. L'objectif est de transformer les recettes mobilisées en équipements, services et activités économiques durables, donnant un contenu concret à la justice territoriale. Diversifier l'économie pour réduire la dépendance à l'exploitation minière La transformation de Kédougou ne peut reposer exclusivement sur l'or, compte tenu de la fluctuation des cours et de l'épuisement prévisible des gisements. La région dispose d'atouts agricoles, pastoraux, agroalimentaires et touristiques qui méritent d'être valorisés. Un programme régional de diversification pourrait privilégier plusieurs stratégies : aménagement de périmètres agricoles et de systèmes d'irrigation adaptés, développement de coopératives et d'entreprises rurales, installation d'unités de transformation agroalimentaire, renforcement des filières d'élevage et des infrastructures commerciales, accès des producteurs au crédit, aux équipements et aux marchés, valorisation du tourisme et de l'écotourisme dans le respect de l'environnement. Cette diversification constitue un investissement stratégique dans l'après-mine. Les ressources non renouvelables doivent contribuer à développer des activités durables, capables de maintenir les emplois et les revenus au-delà de la durée d'exploitation des gisements. L'or doit financer l'avenir économique de Kédougou, et non entretenir sa dépendance. Faire de la gouvernance minière un instrument de responsabilité économique et sociale L'exploitation minière doit être soumise à des exigences renforcées de transparence, de responsabilité sociale, de respect des droits des travailleurs et de protection environnementale. Le suivi des conventions minières et des engagements des entreprises devrait porter notamment sur les obligations fiscales et contractuelles, la qualité des emplois, la sécurité au travail et les droits syndicaux, la formation et le transfert de compétences, la protection des ressources hydriques et des terres agricoles, la réhabilitation des sites et la prévention des risques sanitaires et environnementaux. Une attention particulière doit être accordée à l'orpaillage artisanal. Plutôt que de privilégier exclusivement le contrôle et la répression, l'action publique devrait favoriser sa formalisation progressive, son organisation en coopératives, la sécurisation des sites, l'accès aux équipements et la protection sanitaire et sociale des travailleurs. Des cadres permanents de concertation entre l'État, les exploitants, les syndicats, les collectivités et les communautés riveraines permettraient de prévenir les conflits et d'améliorer la régulation du secteur. Repenser les critères d'évaluation de la richesse et du développement territorial Le taux de pauvreté estimé à 67 % impose de dépasser les seuls indicateurs de production minière. Il convient de distinguer la richesse créée, les revenus conservés localement, les recettes publiques mobilisées et les bénéfices effectivement obtenus par les populations. Un système d'évaluation territorial devrait intégrer la pauvreté, l'accès aux services sociaux, l’emploi décent, la part des marchés attribuée aux entreprises locales, les investissements publics, les revenus des ménages et les coûts environnementaux et sanitaires. La création d'un Observatoire régional des retombées économiques, sociales et environnementales, associant services statistiques, collectivités, universités, syndicats, société civile et entreprises, permettrait de publier régulièrement un tableau de bord fiable et d'orienter les décisions publiques. La transformation de Kédougou exige une redéfinition des responsabilités des acteurs. L'État doit garantir la cohérence des politiques publiques, la protection des droits et la transformation économique des territoires. Les entreprises minières doivent contribuer au développement des compétences, des PME locales, de l’emploi décent et à la prévention des dommages environnementaux. Les collectivités territoriales doivent disposer de moyens réels d'intervention. Les travailleurs et leurs organisations syndicales doivent participer à la gouvernance, au dialogue social et au suivi des engagements. Il serait opportun d'instituer un Cadre régional permanent de concertation sur les ressources naturelles et le développement territorial, chargé de suivre les engagements, d'examiner les difficultés et d'évaluer les retombées de l'exploitation minière. Ce cadre pourrait déboucher sur un Pacte territorial de développement de Kédougou, assorti d'objectifs pluriannuels, d'engagements mesurables et de mécanismes publics de redevabilité. Des recommandations opérationnelles pour passer des engagements aux résultats À court terme : * Réaliser un audit territorial des retombées économiques, fiscales, sociales et environnementales de l'exploitation minière. * Publier une cartographie des investissements, des marchés de sous-traitance, des emplois et des engagements des entreprises. * Installer un cadre régional multipartite de concertation et de suivi. * Élaborer un programme prioritaire de formation et d'insertion professionnelle des jeunes. À moyen terme : * Créer un mécanisme territorial de financement du développement. * Déployer un programme de soutien aux PME et de promotion du contenu local. * Organiser l'orpaillage artisanal en coopératives et sécuriser les sites. * Lancer un programme de diversification agricole, pastorale, agroalimentaire et touristique. * Renforcer les infrastructures de base et les équipements économiques. À long terme : * Instituer un pacte territorial pluriannuel entre l'État, les entreprises, les collectivités et les partenaires sociaux. * Investir dans les compétences, les infrastructures productives et les activités de l'après-mine. * Mettre en place une évaluation indépendante des résultats, notamment en matière de réduction de la pauvreté, d’emploi décent et d'amélioration des conditions de vie. Ces mesures devront être accompagnées d'un calendrier précis, d'une répartition claire des responsabilités institutionnelles et d'une programmation financière réaliste. Faire de Kédougou une référence de la transformation des ressources naturelles en développement humain La situation de Kédougou interpelle l'ensemble du Sénégal sur une question fondamentale : comment garantir que les territoires qui contribuent fortement à la création des richesses nationales bénéficient durablement des fruits de leur contribution ? La réponse ne réside pas uniquement dans l'augmentation des transferts financiers, mais dans la transformation des mécanismes de gouvernance, des politiques d'investissement et des relations économiques entre les entreprises et les territoires. Il s'agit de construire un modèle dans lequel les ressources naturelles financent les infrastructures, les compétences, les entreprises locales et les activités productives ; où les emplois sont décents et accessibles aux populations ; où les collectivités disposent de capacités réelles d'action et où la protection de l'environnement constitue une exigence incontournable. Kédougou pourrait ainsi devenir un laboratoire de développement territorial, démontrant qu'une exploitation responsable des ressources naturelles peut soutenir une économie diversifiée, inclusive et créatrice d’emplois durables. Le véritable défi n'est pas seulement de savoir combien d'or Kédougou produit, mais quelle économie, quelles infrastructures, quelles compétences et quelles perspectives d'avenir cette richesse permet de construire. Faire de la richesse minière un levier de souveraineté économique, de justice territoriale et de dignité humaine : telle devrait être l'ambition collective pour Kédougou. Par Abdoul Karim KEÏTA, Président de l’ONG SADEV Abdoulkarimkeita521@yahoo.com

items.title: Le Président du Conseil au sommet quadripartite sur les questions de paix et de coopération à Oyo (Congo)
items.description: Lomé, 23 nov. (ATOP) – Le Président du Conseil, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, Médiateur désigné de l’Union africaine dans la gestion de la crise dans la région des Grands Lacs, a participé le dimanche 22 novembre à Oyo au Congo, à un sommet quadripartite organisé à l’initiative du Président Denis Sassou N’Guesso. Cette rencontre diplomatique a réuni les dirigeants du Togo, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, du Congo Denis Sassou N’Guesso, de la République Démocratique du Congo (RDC), Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo, du Kenya, William Samoei Ruto. Elle s’inscrit dans la dynamique de concertations régionales autour des questions de paix, de solidarité africaine et de coopération. Le sommet d’Oyo consacre ainsi l’importance de la diplomatie et de la solidarité africaines dans la recherche de réponses concertées aux défis qui affectent le continent. Les présidents ont procédé à un examen approfondi de la situation géopolitique du continent, dans un contexte marqué par des crises sécuritaires et des tensions diplomatiques dans plusieurs régions d’Afrique. Ils ont échangé sur l’état des relations d’amitié et de coopération entre le Kenya et la RDC. Les dirigeants kényan et de la RDC ont souligné la nécessité de consolider les liens entre les deux pays, de restaurer la confiance mutuelle et de promouvoir davantage les valeurs de solidarité et de fraternité entre les peuples. Les présidents Gnassingbé et Sassou N’Guesso ont réaffirmé leur attachement aux principes de souveraineté des Etats, de bon voisinage et de règlement pacifique des crises. Ils ont notamment insisté sur la nécessité de privilégier les voies diplomatiques dans la résolution des crises. Les deux personnalités ont mis en relief l’impératif de renforcer la coopération au sein des mécanismes régionaux chargés des questions de paix, de sécurité et d’intégration, notamment la Conférence internationale sur la région des Grands Lacs (CIRGL) et la Communauté d’Afrique de l’Est (CAE), dont la RDC et le Kenya sont membres. Cette dynamique de coopération vise à favoriser une approche concertée des défis régionaux et à contribuer durablement à la consolidation de la paix et de la stabilité dans les Grands Lacs. Abordant les crises humanitaires, les présidents Gnassingbé et Sassou-N’Guesso ont appelé au renforcement de la coopération entre les pays africains dans la lutte contre la maladie à virus Ebola. Ils ont réitéré leur détermination à donner une traduction concrète aux engagements souscrits dans le cadre du sommet. Les présidents Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo et William Samoei Ruto ont exprimé leur profonde gratitude et leurs remerciements aux dirigeants togolais et congolais pour leur engagement, leur disponibilité et leur contribution à la promotion du dialogue, de la paix, de la solidarité et de la fraternité entre les nations africaines. ATOP/BA/Présidence du Conseil

items.title: Santé : A Kokologho, les langues nationales renforcent la confiance entre soignants et patients
items.description: Depuis le 2 novembre 2026, le ministère de la Santé met en œuvre le mois de la communication sanitaire en langues nationales. À travers cette initiative, le département entend rapprocher davantage les services de santé des populations en leur délivrant des messages de sensibilisation dans les langues qu’elles comprennent. Ce 23 novembre 2026, une équipe de journalistes s’est rendue à Kokologho dans la province du Boulkiemdé pour apprécier le dispositif déployé sur le terrain et recueillir les premières impressions des acteurs et bénéficiaires de cette campagne. À Kokologho, c'est la radio Zamaana FM qui a été retenue pour porter cette initiative. Durant un mois, elle a travaillé en étroite collaboration avec le Centre médical de la localité afin de sensibiliser les populations sur les comportements à adopter pour prévenir les maladies. À travers des émissions radiophoniques interactives, les auditeurs ont également pu bénéficier, en direct et en langue mooré, largement parlée dans la localité, de conseils médicaux et d’informations pratiques sur différentes questions de santé. Alassane Ouédraogo, Médecin-chef du Centre médical de Kokologho Pour le Dr Alassane Ouédraogo, médecin-chef du Centre médical de Kokologho, le recours aux langues nationales dans les échanges entre les agents de santé et les patients présente de nombreux avantages. Il favorise notamment une meilleure compréhension des conseils médicaux et facilite le diagnostic des maladies. « Nous avons une population qui, dans sa majorité, ne comprend pas le français. Lorsqu'elle arrive dans un centre de santé et qu'on s'adresse à elle dans une langue qu'elle ne maîtrise pas, une barrière s'installe immédiatement. En revanche, lorsqu'on lui parle dans sa langue, notamment le mooré ici à Kokologho, on la met automatiquement en confiance », explique-t-il. Le médecin-chef salue ainsi cette initiative du ministère de la Santé, qui devrait, selon lui, contribuer à renforcer la fréquentation des formations sanitaires. Au cours de la campagne, son équipe a notamment animé plusieurs émissions radiophoniques consacrées à différentes thématiques sanitaires, dont la dengue, qui connaît actuellement une recrudescence dans le pays. Ces rendez-vous ont suscité un vif intérêt auprès des auditeurs, qui n'ont pas hésité à intervenir pour obtenir davantage d'informations sur la maladie. « Les gens appelaient de partout pour se renseigner sur la maladie. Et comme les échanges se déroulaient dans une langue qu'ils comprennent, ils ont véritablement participé. Nous pensons donc que les messages de sensibilisation ont été bien reçus », témoigne-t-il. Raïssa Kaboré, Sage-femme au CM de Kokologho Un constat que partage Raïssa Kaboré, sage-femme au Centre médical de Kokologho. Selon elle, les patientes se montrent davantage réceptives lorsque les conseils et les explications leur sont donnés dans leur langue maternelle. Ayant précédemment exercé dans la région du Sahel avant de rejoindre Kokologho, elle dit mesurer pleinement les difficultés que peut engendrer la barrière linguistique dans la relation entre le personnel soignant et les patients. « Quand tu es dans une zone où tu ne comprends pas la langue des populations, tu vas vraiment souffrir. Mais lorsque tu parles une langue que les femmes comprennent, le message passe rapidement et les patientes arrivent à respecter les consignes », souligne-t-elle. La principale difficulté reste toutefois la traduction de certains termes médicaux et techniques dans les langues nationales. Une contrainte que les agents de santé parviennent, selon elle, à contourner en recourant à des expressions et à des explications accessibles aux populations, afin de faciliter la compréhension des messages. Au-delà des professionnels de santé, les bénéficiaires semblent également apprécier cette approche. La patiente Venue tôt dans la matinée au Centre médical de Kokologho pour une consultation prénatale, Fadilatou Kaboré affirme n'avoir rencontré aucune difficulté à échanger avec la sage-femme, celle-ci s'étant exprimée en mooré. Bien qu'elle comprenne le français, elle dit se sentir davantage rassurée lorsque les explications médicales lui sont données dans sa langue maternelle. « Comme la sage-femme s'est exprimée en mooré, je n'ai pas eu de difficulté à comprendre ce qu'elle disait. Je comprends le français, mais je me sens plus en sécurité lorsqu'elle me parle en mooré. Cela me met en confiance », confie-t-elle. Les langues nationales créent un pont entre soignants et patients Lancée le 2 novembre 2026, la campagne se poursuit sur l'ensemble du territoire national. Les premiers chiffres témoignent déjà de sa portée : plus de 185 émissions ont été réalisées à travers le pays, enregistrant plus de 890 appels d'auditeurs et de téléspectateurs. Au total, une trentaine de langues nationales ont été mobilisées pour diffuser les messages de sensibilisation. Oumarou KONATE Minute.bf

items.title: Government moves to ease port congestion, separates shipping line releases from cargo clearance
items.description: The government has directed the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) and terminal operators to separate shipping line release procedures from the cargo clearance process at the ports, in a move to reduce congestion and facilitate international trade. Under the new arrangement, importers who have paid the required duties and completed all customs clearance procedures will be allowed to take delivery of their cargo without waiting for separate release approvals from shipping lines. The measure is expected to eliminate procedural delays, improve the movement of goods and reduce the cost of doing business at the ports. The Head of the Revenue Assurance Department at the Ministry of Finance, Victor Kofi Baidoo, disclosed this at a meeting with members of the Ghana Institute of Freight Forwarders (GIFF) at Tema. The meeting formed part of the ministry’s engagements with freight forwarding stakeholders to discuss measures to improve port operations, address bottlenecks and facilitate trade. Mr Baidoo explained that the directive was part of the government’s efforts to streamline port operations by removing shipping line release procedures from the customs clearance chain. He noted that under the previous arrangement, importers who had paid their duties and completed the necessary customs procedures were still required to obtain separate release approvals from shipping lines before their goods could be evacuated. Under the new system, customs clearance and shipping line transactions will be treated as separate processes. Once Customs has confirmed that the cargo has been duly cleared and the appropriate duties paid, importers can proceed to evacuate their goods while resolving any outstanding transactions with the shipping lines separately. Mr Baidoo said the government had communicated the directive to Customs and terminal operators for implementation. Port Congestion The separation of the two processes is expected to ease pressure on limited storage space at the ports by reducing the time cleared containers remain in the terminals awaiting shipping line approvals. Faster evacuation of cargo could improve container turnaround, create room for incoming consignments and reduce the accumulation of containers within the port. It could also lower demurrage and other avoidable charges incurred by importers, while improving the overall efficiency of the supply chain. Compare Couriers A freight forwarder and leading member of GIFF, Johnny Mantey, welcomed the decision, describing it as a significant step towards addressing congestion at the Tema Port. He said freight forwarders had, over the years, engaged various stakeholders on the need to separate shipping line release procedures from customs clearance, adding that the new arrangement addressed a longstanding concern within the industry. However, Mr Mantey noted that delays in obtaining container releases from some shipping lines remained a major challenge, with importers sometimes having to wait between four and five days to He expressed concern about the increasing number of containers accumulating at the port, particularly empty containers awaiting return to shipping lines. He said the situation was putting pressure on available storage space and could worsen congestion if urgent measures were not taken. Mr Mantey called for greater cooperation from shipping lines to ensure the timely evacuation and return of containers, adding that further engagements would be held with them to address the concerns and prevent the situation from escalating.

items.title: CDD-Ghana’s John Osae-Kwapong blames lack of sanctions for persistent absenteeism among MPs
items.description: A fellow at the Centre for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana), Dr John Osae-Kwapong, has attributed persistent absenteeism among Members of Parliament (MPs) to the failure to hold lawmakers accountable for staying away from parliamentary sittings without reasonable explanations. He argues that the absence of effective sanctions for MPs who disregard parliamentary attendance rules creates little incentive for them to change their behaviour. Speaking on JoyNews AM Show on Monday, November 23, Dr Osae-Kwapong said the continued recurrence of the issue suggested that existing measures had not been effective in ensuring that lawmakers took their attendance obligations seriously. He questioned why absenteeism remained a concern despite repeated discussions about the conduct of MPs, arguing that failure to enforce the rules could encourage further disregard for parliamentary responsibilities. ” If nothing is being done in terms of holding persons accountable for absenting themselves from Parliament without proper explanation or the proper excuse, then no one has the incentive to change behaviour,” he said. Dr Osae-Kwapong maintained that enforcing the existing rules and imposing appropriate consequences on MPs who failed to justify their absence could help reduce the practice. He said lawmakers would be more inclined to comply with attendance requirements if they knew that staying away from parliamentary proceedings without an acceptable reason could attract sanctions. The CDD-Ghana Fellow suggested that the Speaker’s enforcement of parliamentary attendance rules should go beyond expressions of concern to include measures that hold offending MPs responsible for their actions. He noted that such accountability could help address the recurring problem and reinforce the importance of MPs being present to perform their legislative duties. Dr Osae-Kwapong’s comments come amid renewed concerns about absenteeism in Parliament and calls for lawmakers to demonstrate greater commitment to their responsibilities in the House.
