items.title: Africa risks losing control of its media future to foreign AI companies – CJID CEO warns
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID), Dapo Olorunyomi, has warned that Africa risks surrendering control of its information ecosystem to foreign technology companies unless it takes deliberate steps to shape the development and use of artificial intelligence. He says the continent could become increasingly dependent on technologies whose design, priorities and economic benefits are determined elsewhere, raising serious concerns about media independence, data ownership and cultural representation. Speaking at the opening of the 2026 Media and Development Conference in Abuja, Nigeria, on Monday, November 23, Mr. Olorunyomi said the growing influence of artificial intelligence presents both opportunities and serious threats to African journalism. “The question is whether we will shape that transformation to strengthen our institutions or remain consumers of technologies whose design, priorities and economic benefits are determined elsewhere,” he said. He acknowledged that artificial intelligence could significantly improve journalism by reducing the cost of transcription, supporting research, translating information into local languages and analysing large volumes of data. According to him, tasks that previously required substantial financial and technical resources can now be undertaken more efficiently with AI-assisted tools. However, Mr. Olorunyomi cautioned that the same technology could be exploited to spread misinformation, distort reality and manipulate public opinion. “AI can generate falsehoods, reproduce historical biases and flood information spaces with synthetic text, audio, images and videos at a speed that overwhelms verification,” he warned. He expressed particular concern about the threat AI-generated content poses to democratic processes, especially during elections when manipulated audio and video recordings can spread rapidly before their authenticity is established. Mr. Olorunyomi argued that the speed at which false information circulates is increasingly outpacing the capacity of journalists and independent institutions to verify facts. “We are living in a time when the speed of deception can exceed the capacity of institutions to establish the truth,” he said. Beyond misinformation, the CJID Chief Executive raised concerns about the underrepresentation of African languages, cultural experiences and local knowledge in the datasets used to develop artificial intelligence systems. He warned that this could affect the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated information and further marginalise African societies in the emerging digital economy. Mr. Olorunyomi called on African media organisations to introduce clear editorial policies governing the use of artificial intelligence in news production. He insisted that machine-generated materials must undergo rigorous human verification, while journalists must protect confidential sources, sensitive data and editorial independence. “Automation and convenience must never displace professional judgement. Artificial intelligence must serve journalism, not the other way around,” he stressed. He also urged African governments, universities, research institutions and technology companies to invest in local AI capabilities and digital infrastructure to ensure the continent participates meaningfully in developing emerging technologies. Mr. Olorunyomi maintained that Africa must not remain a passive consumer of technological innovations that increasingly shape its political, economic and democratic future. “Africa must become an active architect, owner and beneficiary of its own digital future,” he said. The 2026 Media and Development Conference, organised by CJID, is being held under the theme “Media, Technology and the Future of Democratic Societies,” with discussions focusing on the implications of emerging technologies for journalism, information integrity and democracy.

items.title: Senegal to know fate of AFCON title appeal Tuesday – CAS
items.description: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) announced that a verdict on Senegal’s appeal of the decision to strip them of the Africa Cup of Nations title in favour of Morocco will come on Tuesday. CAS’s ruling comes after a hearing of the case, over a chaotic AFCON final in January, which took place behind closed doors at its headquarters in Lausanne on October 8. “The parties have been notified that the CAS decision will be rendered Tuesday 24 November 2026 in the course of the afternoon (GMT),” CAS said in a short statement on Monday. At the January 18 final in Rabat, Senegal won 1-0 thanks to Pape Gueye’s extra-time goal, but the occasion was marred near the end of normal time when many Senegal players walked off the pitch in protest at the decision to award Morocco a penalty with the match still goalless. Some Senegalese supporters also attempted a pitch invasion, and the game was held up for almost 20 minutes before the Senegal players returned. In March, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) overturned that result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title. In response, the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the ruling as the “most blatant administrative robbery in the history of our sport”. The Senegal team even paraded the trophy to their supporters in Paris at the end of March. The post Senegal to know fate of AFCON title appeal Tuesday – CAS appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Issoufou Dayo revient, ce que cela change pour les Étalons
items.description: Le retour d’Issoufou Dayo n’est pas une simple convocation de plus. À 35 ans, le défenseur central du Wydad AC a décidé de sortir de sa retraite internationale, annoncée en janvier 2026 après la CAN 2025. Amir Abdou l’a retenu dans un groupe de 25 joueurs, ouvrant une nouvelle étape dans sa carrière internationale. Pour ceux qui consultent 1xBet pour les paris sportifs afin d’analyser les rencontres du Burkina Faso, cette décision change surtout la lecture du secteur défensif. Dayo apporte de l’expérience, mais sa présence ne garantit pas une place de titulaire. Un retour neuf mois après la CAN Dayo avait disputé les 90 minutes de l’élimination 3-0 contre la Côte d’Ivoire, le 6 janvier 2026, en huitième de finale de la CAN. Quelques jours plus tard, il avait annoncé la fin de sa carrière internationale. Amir Abdou a ensuite expliqué s’être déplacé au Maroc pour échanger avec lui. Le sélectionneur a mis en avant ses performances en club et son influence dans le groupe, tout en précisant qu’il devrait accepter la concurrence. Avec plus de 70 sélections, Dayo connaît les grandes compétitions africaines. Mais il retrouve une défense déjà structurée autour de plusieurs options, dont Edmond Tapsoba et Nasser Djiga dans l’axe, avec Issa Kaboré, Arsène Kouassi et Rachide Gnanou pour élargir les possibilités. Pourquoi son profil reste utile Le rappel de Dayo ne répond pas seulement à une question de nombre. Son expérience du placement, des duels et de la gestion des différentes phases d’un match peut être utile lorsque le Burkina Faso doit défendre un avantage ou affronter une équipe qui utilise beaucoup les centres et le jeu direct. Son retour offre aussi une solution supplémentaire en cas d’absence ou de changement tactique. Amir Abdou peut privilégier une charnière plus expérimentée, davantage de mobilité ou une organisation différente selon l’adversaire. Cette souplesse compte dans une campagne où les exigences peuvent changer rapidement d’un match à l’autre. La concurrence reste ouverte en défense Amir Abdou n’a pas présenté ce rappel comme un retour automatique dans le onze. Dayo devra gagner sa place. Plusieurs options existent : l’associer à Tapsoba ou Djiga dans une défense à deux ; l’intégrer à une ligne de trois ; utiliser son expérience dans certaines phases de match ; renforcer la communication au sein du groupe. Le choix dépendra surtout de la forme, de la complémentarité et du plan de jeu. Une association expérimentée n’est pas automatiquement plus efficace qu’une charnière déjà habituée à évoluer ensemble. Ce que son retour change pour les paris Le retour d’un joueur aussi identifié à la sélection peut influencer la perception du Burkina Faso, mais il ne suffit pas à modifier à lui seul la lecture d’un marché. La première information à vérifier reste la composition officielle. Si Dayo débute, son partenaire dans l’axe et le système choisi auront un impact direct sur les marchés liés au résultat, aux buts encaissés ou au clean sheet. Une défense à deux avec Tapsoba ne présente pas les mêmes caractéristiques qu’une ligne de trois incluant Djiga. La qualité de l’adversaire et les performances défensives récentes restent également essentielles. Un défenseur expérimenté peut améliorer l’organisation sans faire disparaître les occasions concédées. À l’approche du coup d’envoi, les marchés proposés sur 1xBet APK peuvent évoluer lorsque compositions et absences sont confirmées. Le retour de Dayo peut donc peser sur certaines cotes, sans suffire à justifier à lui seul un pari sur le vainqueur ou le total de buts. Son temps de jeu, sa condition physique et ses automatismes avec ses partenaires comptent finalement davantage que sa réputation ou son nombre de sélections. Une option supplémentaire pour Amir Abdou L’intérêt du retour de Dayo dépasse un seul match. Le Burkina Faso doit pouvoir adapter sa défense à différents scénarios : protéger un avantage, défendre plus haut ou gérer davantage de transitions. L’expérience de Dayo donne au sélectionneur une solution supplémentaire pour modifier son organisation. Sa communication et sa lecture du jeu peuvent également être utiles lorsque la composition change. L’enjeu n’est donc pas seulement de savoir s’il sera titulaire, mais de déterminer dans quelles situations son profil complète le mieux ceux des autres défenseurs. Un retour qui ne bouleverse pas tout Le retour de Dayo ne signifie pas que le Burkina Faso revient à son ancienne défense. Amir Abdou conserve plusieurs joueurs déjà intégrés à son organisation et ajoute simplement une option expérimentée. À 35 ans, Dayo n’a pas été rappelé uniquement pour son passé avec les Étalons. Le sélectionneur a aussi mis en avant ses performances en club et son influence dans le groupe. La suite dépendra de sa forme et de la concurrence. Titulaire ou remplaçant, Dayo élargit surtout les choix disponibles pour une sélection qui cherche à consolider son organisation défensive. items.title: Algérie – Kazakhstan : accord aérien pour jusqu’à 14 vols par semaine
items.description: L’Algérie et le Kazakhstan sont convenus d’autoriser leurs compagnies aériennes d’effectuer jusqu’à 14 liaisons par semaine entre les deux pays. Le directeur de l’Agence nationale de l’aviation civile, Hassane Boulfelfel et le président du Comité de l’aviation civile du Kazakhstan Saltanat Tompiyeva, ont signé un protocole d’accord définissant le cadre du développement de la connectivité aérienne, rapporte l'agence de presse Qazinform. L’accord, signé dimanche 22 novembre à Montréal, en marge de la 7 e conférence mondiale sur le transport aérien de l'OACI, prévoit notamment « la possibilité, pour les transporteurs aériens désignés par chaque partie, d’assurer jusqu’à 14 liaisons hebdomadaires ». Le Kazakhstan et l'Algérie, selon la même source, ont également paraphé un projet d'accord sur les services aériens, destiné à fixer le cadre juridique nécessaire au lancement de vols réguliers entre les deux pays. Air Algérie : une ligne Alger – Astana en projet L’ambassadeur du Kazakhstan à Alger, Anuarbek Akhmetov, avait annoncé en octobre dernier, qu’une ligne directe entre Alger et Astana était en cours de planification. La ligne devrait être exploitée par Air Algérie, a-t-il ajouté. Selon le diplomate, l’établissement d’une ligne directe entre les deux pays permettra de faciliter les déplacements des hommes d’affaires. Air Algérie a procédé, récemment, à l’élargissement de son réseau international à travers le lancement de 5 nouvelles lignes vers l'Afrique et l'Asie. Il est question de 4 nouvelles destinations vers les pays africains, à savoir Conakry (25 octobre), Brazzaville et Lagos (26 octobre) et Tripoli (28 octobre). Pour l’Asie, Air Algérie a ouvert une liaison Alger-Shanghai qui s’ajoute aux liaisons vers Pékin et Guangzhou. items.title: Ghana and Ukraine: Different histories, one shared struggle for freedom and dignity
items.description: On Ukraine’s Day of Dignity and Freedom, a reflection on two nations that have fought to preserve their identity, reclaim their heritage and determine their own future. On 21 November, Ukraine marks the Day of Dignity and Freedom, commemorating two defining moments in its modern history: the Orange Revolution of 2004 and the Revolution of Dignity, which began in 2013. Both reflected the determination of Ukrainians to defend their freedom, democracy and right to decide the future of their country. For Ghanaians, the meaning of this day may be particularly familiar. Ghana’s own history is a story of the struggle against colonial rule, the achievement of independence and the determination to preserve national identity, culture and heritage despite attempts by foreign powers to control them. The historical experiences of Ghana and Ukraine were different. Ghana fought against European colonial rule, while Ukraine endured centuries of imperial domination, particularly under the Russian Empire and later the Soviet system. Yet both nations understand that independence means more than a change in political status. It means having the freedom to preserve one’s identity and determine one’s own future. Ghana’s struggle for independence was a landmark in African history. Long before European colonial rule, the territory of present-day Ghana was home to established kingdoms and communities, including the powerful Ashanti Empire, with their own political institutions, traditions and cultural heritage. Despite colonial rule, the people of the Gold Coast continued to defend their interests and aspirations for self-government. On 6 March 1957, under the leadership of Dr Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African country to achieve independence in the post-war era. Its independence inspired liberation movements across the continent. Nkrumah believed that Ghana’s freedom would have little meaning unless it contributed to the liberation of Africa as a whole. Ghana consequently became an important voice for African unity and the right of peoples to govern themselves. Ukraine’s history followed a different path. Its historical roots go back more than a thousand years to Kyivan Rus, a powerful medieval state with Kyiv as its political, cultural and spiritual centre. At that time, Moscow did not yet exist as a political centre. Centuries later, however, Moscow began claiming the historical legacy of Kyivan Rus, gradually presenting itself as its principal and eventually exclusive heir. This was not simply a historical disagreement. It became part of a wider imperial policy: appropriating another nation’s history and cultural heritage while denying that nation’s right to exist independently. The Russian Empire and later Soviet authorities repeatedly restricted the Ukrainian language, culture and national traditions. Ukrainian writers, intellectuals, artists and other cultural figures were persecuted, imprisoned and killed. The aim was not only to control the territory but also to weaken the national identity that distinguished Ukrainians from the empire ruling them. This contradiction may be particularly easy to understand in Ghana, where the struggle to recover cultural artefacts taken during colonial rule remains an important issue of national dignity and historical justice. President John Dramani Mahama has offered a simple but powerful way of explaining this principle. He compared the continued possession of stolen property to a stolen watch: if someone steals your watch and later passes it on to an heir, it does not stop being stolen property simply because another generation has inherited it. Ivan Lukachuk, Chargé d’Affaires a.i. of Ukraine in the Republic of Ghana The same principle applies to history and cultural heritage. The passage of time does not turn appropriation into legitimate ownership. Nor does passing stolen property from one generation to another change the fact that it was taken from someone else. So-called Russia has followed this imperial pattern with Ukraine. It has appropriated the historical legacy of Kyivan Rus and presented Ukrainian cultural achievements as part of an exclusively Russian heritage, while persecuting generations of Ukrainians for preserving their own language, traditions and identity. In effect, Moscow sought not only to claim Ukraine’s historical inheritance but also to silence the people who created and preserved it. Just as Ghana seeks the return of its looted cultural treasures, Ukraine has the right to reclaim and protect its own history and cultural identity. A nation’s heritage belongs to the people who created it, not to an empire that claims ownership over it. Nor was Ukraine the only nation to experience this kind of imperial domination. The Russian Empire incorporated numerous peoples and territories, many of whose languages, cultures and political aspirations were suppressed. Even today, the Russian state uses imperial historical narratives to justify its influence over neighbouring nations and question their right to make independent choices. Ukraine’s struggle for statehood continued through many difficult periods. Even when it became a founding member of the United Nations in 1945, represented by the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, it did not enjoy genuine political independence. Its international activities remained largely controlled by Moscow. Ukraine finally declared independence on 24 August 1991, a decision confirmed by an overwhelming majority of citizens in the nationwide referendum of 1 December that year. The history of Ghanaian-Ukrainian relations also goes back further than the establishment of diplomatic ties. Ghana’s first President, Kwame Nkrumah, visited Kyiv on 18–19 July 1961 and later travelled to Crimea with his family. At the time, Ukraine was still part of the Soviet Union. During Nkrumah’s presidency, Ghana pursued an ambitious programme of industrialisation, infrastructure development, education and economic transformation. Soviet-Ghanaian cooperation included projects in industry, construction, energy and agriculture. These initiatives were undertaken within the framework of Ghana’s relations with the Soviet Union, rather than with an independent Ukrainian state. There was, however, an important historical contrast: while Ghana was using its newly gained independence to shape its own development, Ukraine remained within a political system where major decisions about its future were made outside the country. A new chapter began in 1991. Ghana recognised Ukraine’s independence on 22 April 1992, and diplomatic relations were established on 17 June 1992. Since then, the two countries have developed relations based on equality and mutual respect. The visit of Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba to Ghana in October 2022 and the opening of the Ukrainian Embassy in Accra at the end of 2023 gave new momentum to bilateral cooperation. The Revolution of Dignity, which began on 21 November 2013, was triggered by the Ukrainian government’s decision to suspend preparations for signing an Association Agreement with the European Union. What started as a protest against that decision grew into a nationwide movement in defence of democratic rights, human dignity and Ukraine’s sovereign right to choose its own direction. For Ukrainians, it was another chapter in a much longer struggle to preserve their identity and independence. Today, these principles are being tested once again. Russia’s full-scale aggression against Ukraine is an attempt to undermine the country’s sovereignty, seize its territory and deny its people the right to determine their own future. The war also targets Ukraine’s cultural heritage, historical memory and national identity. The experiences of Ghana and Ukraine should not be equated. Their historical paths were different. But both demonstrate a fundamental truth: no nation should have its history, identity or future imposed by an external power. This principle lies at the heart of the United Nations Charter and the international order that Ghana and Ukraine, as sovereign states, have committed themselves to uphold. The historical connection between Ghana and Ukraine should not remain simply a matter of remembrance. It can serve as a foundation for a stronger partnership. Agriculture and food security offer particularly promising opportunities. Ukraine has extensive experience in grain production, agricultural technologies, food processing and logistics. Ghana has considerable agricultural potential and a clear ambition to increase domestic production and add value to its agricultural output. Education is another important bridge. Generations of Ghanaian students have studied in Ukraine, creating professional and personal connections between the two societies. Renewed academic exchanges, vocational training and cooperation between universities could strengthen these ties. There is also considerable potential in trade, technology, infrastructure and cooperation within international organisations. The opening of Ukraine’s Embassy in Accra has created new opportunities to turn these ambitions into concrete results. Ghana’s independence remains one of the landmark achievements in Africa’s history. Ukraine’s journey from imperial domination to independence, and its ongoing defence of sovereignty, form another story of a nation’s determination to be free. Our histories are not the same, but they offer an important basis for mutual understanding. Ghana knows the importance of reclaiming its cultural heritage and protecting its national dignity. Ukraine knows what it means to defend its history, identity and right to exist in the face of an imperial power seeking to deny them. On Ukraine’s Day of Dignity and Freedom, we recall a principle meaningful to every nation, large or small: freedom is not simply the absence of foreign rule. It is the ability to preserve one’s history, culture and identity, make independent decisions and build a future according to the will of one’s own people. Different historical paths. One shared belief in freedom, dignity and the right of every nation to own its history and choose its own future. – By: Ivan Lukachuk, Chargé d’Affaires a.i. of Ukraine in the Republic of Ghana.

items.title: World: Zero-dose children cannot become the next global health crisis – Save the Children
items.description: Country: World Source: Save the Children Despite decades of progress, millions of children continue to miss out on life-saving immunisations, putting them at greater risk of preventable disease, disability and death and leaving the world off track to meet its commitment to halving number of zero-dose children and ending the preventable deaths of children under the age of five. ADDIS ABABA, 23 November 2026 - Children who have never received a single vaccine must remain a priority for all stakeholders, Save the Children said today as leaders gather for the 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026). Despite decades of progress, millions of children continue to miss out on life-saving immunisations, putting them at greater risk of preventable disease, disability and death and leaving the world off track to meet its commitment to halving number of zero-dose children and ending the preventable deaths of children under the age of five. Samy Ahmar, Head of Global Health at Save the Children UK who is attending CPHIA this week said: "Vaccines are one of the greatest public health achievements in history, yet millions of children are still missing out on this life-saving protection. Across Africa and around the world, the children most likely to be missed are often those facing the greatest barriers to healthcare: children living in conflict, displacement, multidimensional poverty, urban poor and remote communities. “Unvaccinated children are often affected by multiple, overlapping deprivations, including malnutrition and a lack of access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services. These factors weaken immune systems and increase susceptibility to infection. Together, they create a perfect storm in which the same children face a heightened risk of disease, severe illness, and death. "The world has set ambitious goals to reach more children with immunisation and cut the number of zero-dose children in half and end the preventable deaths of children under the age of five, but we remain off track. At a time of growing financial pressure on countries and increasing strain on health systems, we cannot allow children to die from causes that we can easily prevent due to a lack of political will. Reaching every child with vaccines is not only a health imperative, but also a test of our collective commitment to equity. "As leaders gather at CPHIA, we have an opportunity to reset our focus on what matters most: ensuring health systems are sustainably financed, and communities are empowered to help shape solutions that work for them. Progress will depend on moving beyond fragmented approaches and international donors and partners aligning behind country-led priorities that can deliver for children over the long term, in line with the recommendations of the Accra Reset. The Gavi Leap is an example of how global health institutions can make concrete steps towards this goal for greater health sovereignty." "Through Save the Children’s work with partners, including governments and communities around the world, we have seen that zero-dose children can be reached with vaccines and other essential health services when barriers are understood and addressed. The challenge is not knowing what works. The challenge is finding stronger political will, financing and accountability to bring those solutions to the scale children need. "No child should die from a disease that we know how to prevent. As governments, donors, health institutions and partners meet in Addis Ababa, we must all seize this moment to turn ambition into action, because for every under vaccinated child, the cost of inaction is far too high." Anab and her colleagues, Maryam and Kaltun, deliver life-saving vaccinations against diseases including diphtheria, pneumonia and measles to some of Somalia’s hardest-to-reach communities. Hundreds of thousands of children remain unvaccinated across the country. If children miss these vital vaccines before the age of five, they may never receive protection against these life-threatening diseases. Last year, Save the Children’s integrated health outreach programme reached more than 135,000 children, with over 43,000 receiving their first vaccination and 26,000 treated for other life-threatening illnesses. Working alongside community mobilisers Mohamud and Bisharo, the team travels up to 300 kilometres by ambulance, donkey and on foot to reach families beyond the reach of health facilities. Maintaining the cold chain every step of the way, they bring vaccinations, malnutrition screening and essential healthcare directly to children who might otherwise go without. Brian Otieno/ Save the Children Health worker Anab and her colleagues Maryam and Kaltun travel by ambulance, on foot and by donkey to bring routine vaccines to remote and nomadic families in Puntland, Somalia. The hardest part of the job is not the distance. It is trust, and they are winning it. The polio vaccination campaign in Gaza has begun on 1 September following the arrival of 1.26 million doses of OPV2 vaccines and 500 insulated vaccine carriers. Save the Children's Primary Health Care Centre (PHCC) in Deir Al-Balah has been designated as one of the key vaccination sites (there are 51 in total ). We are overseeing site operations, coordinating community outreach, and ensuring an efficient vaccination process to maximise coverage quickly. Additionally, Save the Children is disseminating health promotion messages to educate communities about preventing polio and other infectious diseases. On Sunday 1 September, 1,825 children were vaccinated in our clinic. The campaign will run for two more days (today and tomorrow), followed by a "follow-up" day for anyone missed. Tens of thousands of children have missed routine immunizations, and many newborns received none at all after 16 months of bombardment by Israeli forces and restrictions on entry of medical supplies brought Gaza’s healthcare system to the brink and saw polio re-emerge for the first time in 25 years. The measles outbreak is affecting all eight divisions in Bangladesh, prompting an emergency vaccination campaign across the country. In the last month, nearly 18 million children have been reached with at least one dose of the vaccine, according to government data.

items.title: Ghanaian photography duo TwinsDntBeg announces collaboration with Canon
items.description: Ghanaian photography and videography duo TwinsDntBeg has announced a collaboration with global imaging brand Canon, marking another milestone in the career of the twin brothers, whose work has taken them from local events to international creative platforms. The announcement, made on November 19, 2026, is expected to open a new chapter for the duo, who say they intend to use the collaboration to share their experience and help develop the next generation of African photographers, filmmakers and content creators. Through the partnership, the brothers plan to create visual stories and share lessons drawn from years of working behind the camera, with a focus on encouraging young creatives to document their communities and tell authentic African stories. “We started with a dream,” the duo said. “Through every event we covered, every challenge, and every opportunity, we kept pushing the boundaries.” TwinsDntBeg is also exploring plans for a masterclass aimed at emerging creatives. The proposed session would draw on practical experiences from their assignments, including how to plan shoots, manage the pressure of covering live events and turn photographs and video footage into compelling visual stories. Although details of the Canon collaboration have not yet been fully outlined, the announcement places the Ghanaian creatives alongside a global imaging brand and provides a platform for them to share their expertise with a wider community of content creators. From campus events to international assignments TwinsDntBeg is made up of twin brothers Emmanuel Appiah-Gyan and Samuel Appiah Gyan, who operate under the brand name Swag of Africa Studios. In an interview published by My Story Magazine in 2018, the brothers traced their interest in photography to their experiences organising events while at university. They said they became interested in photography after recognising that the quality of images produced at their events did not meet their expectations. Their move into professional photography followed an opportunity to work on the movie set of Cursed One, which they said exposed them to cinematography and helped shape their creative direction. The brothers have since developed a portfolio covering photography, videography, public relations, advertising and digital content creation. Their work has included assignments involving prominent Ghanaian personalities, entertainment figures and public events. They have also worked on projects outside Ghana, building a reputation for documenting African people, culture and events through photography and film. Exhibitions and international recognition The duo has also used exhibitions and creative platforms to showcase their work beyond commissioned assignments. In April 2022, they held their first photo exhibition at the residence of the French Ambassador to Ghana, in collaboration with the French Embassy and Lakeside Village. The exhibition featured photographs and creative projects spanning fashion, media and lifestyle. A second exhibition in April 2024 at the Country Club, Trasacco Valley, Accra, brought together photography, music and networking. The works on display included landscapes and portraits exploring different aspects of life and culture. Their growing profile has also taken them into international discussions on Africa’s creative development. In 2024, they were invited as panellists at the Warwick Africa Summit in the United Kingdom, where they were expected to contribute perspectives on African identity, culture and storytelling. They were subsequently named among the headline speakers for the summit’s 10th anniversary edition in February 2026, alongside Grammy Award-winning artiste Eve. In another notable achievement, TwinsDntBeg received a nomination for Music Film of the Year at the 2025 Black Stars International Film Festival for their visual collaboration with Ghanaian musician Rocky Dawuni on the project Rise. The film used images of Ghanaian landscapes and everyday life to complement the song’s themes of resilience, unity and spiritual awakening. The nomination highlighted the duo’s work beyond event photography and its growing involvement in visual storytelling and music-film production. Developing the next generation The proposed masterclass under the Canon collaboration could extend the brothers’ work into skills development, giving young creatives access to practical lessons from their experience in the industry. The duo says it wants to help emerging photographers and filmmakers understand the demands of professional assignments, from preparation and equipment choices to working under pressure and delivering finished content. For the brothers, the wider ambition is to encourage African creatives to tell stories from their own communities and present the continent through images that reflect its people, cultures and experiences. TwinsDntBeg operates under Swag of Africa Studios, a creative outfit that brings together photographers, videographers, bloggers and graphic designers. The Canon collaboration is expected to provide another platform for the duo to advance that ambition while sharing its experience with a new generation of visual storytellers.

items.title: Tinubu directed me to secure Yorubaland against terrorists – Igboho
items.description: …says President called for collaboration with security agencies to protect rural communities, urban centres, forests By Adeola Badru Yoruba nation activist and founder of the Iru Ekun Security Network, Chief Sunday Adeyemo, popularly known as Sunday Igboho, has disclosed that President Bola Tinubu directed him to sustain security operations across Yorubaland, with particular emphasis on protecting rural communities, urban centres and forests against terrorists from neighbouring African countries. Igboho said the president gave the directive during a brief discussion lasting about five minutes inside his official car shortly after the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally held at Mapo Hall, Ibadan, the Oyo State capital, on Saturday. According to him, Tinubu also emphasised the need for the Iru Ekun Security Network to maintain effective collaboration with the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigerian Army, the Department of State Services (DSS) and other relevant security agencies to prevent the infiltration of terrorists and other criminal elements into the South-West. Igboho disclosed this in a statement issued by his media office on Monday, which quoted him as saying that the President’s directive was aimed at strengthening security across the region, particularly in rural settlements, urban centres and forest reserves. He said, “After the Ibadan Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) rally on Saturday, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu called me into his car and instructed me to continue working with security agencies to ensure peace and stability in the South-West.” “I was honoured by our President on Saturday when I had a brief discussion with him inside his official car before the presidential convoy moved out of the ancient Mapo Hall premises, Ibadan.” “It vividly shows that Mr. President values our selfless efforts to galvanise and improve security and safety of our people.” The Yoruba activist said the discussion, although brief, highlighted the importance the president attached to the security of the Southwest and the continued activities of the homegrown security initiative. “Our discussion lasted for about five minutes. Mr President directed that we must sustain our operations by securing rural communities, urban centres and our forests in Yorubaland against terrorists from neighbouring African countries,” he said. Igboho added that Tinubu specifically stressed the importance of cooperation between the Iru Ekun Security Network and established security agencies in tackling criminal activities across the region. He said the president also directed the operatives to pay particular attention to agrarian communities and forest reserves, which could be vulnerable to infiltration by terrorists and other criminal groups. “Mr President emphasised that Iru Ekun cooperation with all security agencies is germane to tackle criminalities in Yorubaland, including our agrarian settlements and forest reserves.” “He said we should monitor all terrains with a view to preventing infiltration by terrorists from Lake Chad, Mali and other African countries,” he stated. Igboho further disclosed that the President instructed the security network to provide protection for all Nigerians within its areas of operation, irrespective of their ethnic, religious or political affiliations. According to him, Tinubu also stressed the need for the network to notify the relevant security agencies before carrying out its operations in order to ensure effective coordination and achieve the desired results. “We were also instructed to provide security to all Nigerians within our jurisdictions, regardless of ethnic, religion and political divides. “He stressed that our security duties must be carried out by informing security agencies ahead such that positive results and impacts can be achieved in restoring the confidence of the people in government’s responsibility of providing security for the citizenry,” the statement quoted Igboho as saying.” Igboho said the brief encounter with Tinubu demonstrated the president’s recognition of the efforts of local security initiatives in supporting the protection of lives and property, while stressing that such efforts must remain coordinated with established security agencies. He added that the directive was not limited to any particular community or group but covered all Nigerians within the operational areas of the Iru Ekun Security Network, regardless of their ethnic, religious or political differences. Igboho reiterated the importance of collaboration between the network and conventional security agencies, particularly in securing vulnerable communities and preventing the infiltration of terrorists from neighbouring African countries. He added that the security network would continue to work towards restoring public confidence in the government’s responsibility to protect citizens and maintain peace across Yorubaland. The post Tinubu directed me to secure Yorubaland against terrorists – Igboho appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Medvedev évoque une riposte préventive en cas de livraison d'armes nucléaires à l'Ukraine
items.description: Dans un article intitule « Souverainete de l'etat et armes nucleaires : aspects de droit international relatifs a la securite nationale » , le vice-president du Conseil de securite russe, Dmitri Medvedev, a mis en garde contre toute livraison d'armes nucleaires a Kiev, brandissant la menace d'une frappe russe preventive. Dans son article, l'ancien president russe a estime qu'il etait evident que, jusqu'a present, l'evolution de la crise ukrainienne n'avait pas cree de situation necessitant directement le recours a des armes de destruction massive. Toutefois, dans une note de bas de page, il a laisse entrevoir la possibilite d'actions preventives de la part de la Russie en cas de transfert de telles armes a l'Ukraine. « Bien que la version actuelle des "Principes de la politique d'etat de la Federation de Russie dans le domaine de la dissuasion nucleaire" ne prevoie pas directement l'utilisation preventive d'armes nucleaires, il convient d'en conclure que les livraisons (ouvertes ou secretes) d'armes nucleaires par l'Occident au regime de Kiev pourraient obliger la Russie a prendre une decision preventive en vue de neutraliser cette menace », a indique Dmitri Medvedev. Medvedev a oppose les fondements juridiques internationaux justifiant le recours a la force militaire a l'encontre de l'Iran et de l'Ukraine. Selon lui, les etats-Unis et Israel n'avaient aucun fondement juridique pour lancer des frappes contre l'Iran en raison de son programme nucleaire. Il a quant a lui qualifie l'operation militaire speciale russe en Ukraine de mesure preventive de legitime defense, conforme a l'article 51 de la Charte des Nations unies, qui consacre le droit inalienable des etats a la legitime defense, individuelle ou collective. Depuis 2021, plusieurs responsables ukrainiens remettent ouvertement en cause l'abandon de l'arsenal nucleaire herite de l'URSS, la reference a l'arme nucleaire s'etant progressivement imposee comme un instrument de pression diplomatique. En mars dernier, Volodymyr Zelensky a notamment exige soit l'arme atomique, soit l'adhesion a l'OTAN, justifiant cette demande par la necessite de « garantir sa securite ». Moscou faisait etat de tentatives du regime de Kiev de se procurer des armes de destruction massive en secret et sans faire de vagues. Ainsi, en fevrier dernier, le Service de renseignement exterieur russe a indique que Paris et Londres, conscients des maigres chances de succes de l'Ukraine sur le champ de bataille, avaient l'intention de l'equiper d'armes nucleaires ou d'une « bombe sale », en envisageant de transferer discretement a Kiev des composants, des equipements et des technologies europeens dans ce domaine. La position de la Russie sur cette question reste inebranlable. Le president russe, Vladimir Poutine, a declare que Moscou ne permettrait pas que Kiev se dote de l'arme atomique. Il a qualifie cela de menace a laquelle la Russie repondrait de maniere appropriee. La porte-parole du ministere russe des Affaires etrangeres, Maria Zakharova, a quant a elle averti que le transfert d'armes nucleaires a Kiev constituerait une escalade extreme , saperait le regime de non-proliferation et violerait les obligations prevues par le Traite de non-proliferation.

items.title: Touba : un programme de rénovation et de restructuration urbaine annoncé
items.description: Le ministre de l'Urbanisme, des Collectivités territoriales et de l'Aménagement des territoires, Moussa Bala Fofana, a annoncé, samedi 21 novembre 2026, un projet de rénovation et de restructuration urbaine de la ville de Touba. Il a fait cette déclaration durant l'inauguration de l'école Nouroul Makhidi. MBACKÉ- La ville de Touba pourrait bientôt bénéficier d'un vaste programme de rénovation et de restructuration urbaine. L'annonce a été faite, samedi, par le ministre de l'Urbanisme, des Collectivités territoriales et de l'Aménagement des territoires, Moussa Bala Fofana, lors de l'inauguration de l'école Nouroul Makhidi, située dans le quartier de Darou Marnane. Selon lui, le projet est à un stade très avancé de son élaboration. « Nous sommes en train de travailler sur un programme de rénovation et de restructuration urbaine pour Touba », a déclaré le ministre. Cette initiative intervient dans un contexte marqué par une forte croissance démographique et une urbanisation rapide de la capitale du mouridisme. À ces défis, s'ajoutent les difficultés liées à l'assainissement qui exposent régulièrement plusieurs quartiers aux inondations durant l'hivernage. Selon Moussa Bala Fofana, le projet sera inscrit dans le cadre du Programme national de renouveau urbain et d'habitat souverain. Il s'agit, a-t-il expliqué, « de mieux planifier le développement de Touba et d'anticiper les besoins d'une ville confrontée à une expansion démographique et urbaine importante ». Le ministre a également évoqué la perspective d'investissements directs étrangers structurés pour accompagner le développement de la cité de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba. S'exprimant sur l'école Nouroul Makhidi dont il venait de procéder à l'inauguration, Moussa Bala Fofana a salué une réalisation rendue possible grâce aux dons et au volontariat. Il y voit une illustration de l'engagement citoyen dans la prise en charge des besoins des populations. L'établissement, qui combine enseignement religieux et général, participe, à l’en croire, à la formation d'une jeunesse instruite, autonome et attachée aux valeurs spirituelles et culturelles. Birane DIOP (Correspondant)

items.title: License-Plate Readers Are Accelerating ICE’s Crackdown
items.description: S unday is usually a slow day for ICE. There are fewer officers on duty. The people they want to arrest are more likely to stay indoors. The agency’s arrest numbers tend to dip, and that can put pressure on the officers working a Sunday shift. This appears to have been the case on September 20 in Austin, when an ICE officer identified in court filings as D.F. pulled up behind a blue Toyota Corolla around midday. The car was parked outside a restaurant with its hazard lights flashing—a telltale sign of a delivery driver making a pickup. Officer D.F., who was driving an unmarked SUV, pointed his automated license-plate reader at the Corolla. D.F. learned that the vehicle was registered to Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan with a pending deportation order. D.F. and his partner that day, identified as L.G., attempted to stop and question Garcés Pérez, but he drove away, clipping L.G. with his side mirror. The officers pursued the Corolla, and when L.G. tried to stop the vehicle a second time, he drew his weapon and shot Garcés Pérez in the back. (L.G. was not using a body camera , in violation of ICE policy, and the sequence of events immediately leading up to the gunfire was not recorded.) Garcés Pérez survived, but he has been charged with assaulting a federal officer and remains in custody. During a federal-court hearing 10 days later, the Department of Homeland Security special agent Rick Bazan, who investigated the shooting, testified that D.F. and L.G. were “doing random checks on vehicles and at random places” that Sunday. The officers were looking for people they could arrest, Bazan said in an audio recording of the proceeding obtained by Austin’s KUT News , describing those tactics as routine. The shooting was one of several in recent months that have generated outrage over ICE’s use of force during vehicle stops. Officers fatally shot a 52-year-old contractor named Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston on July 7, and an ICE officer in Maine killed another delivery driver, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, in his car six days later. Plate readers were used by officers in both incidents, a senior ICE official told me. The killings, and other shootings since, prompted ICE leaders to order more training and require the use of body cameras. But the agency has already placed powerful new technologies into officers’ hands and encouraged their aggressive deployment. It’s hard to see how the agency will be able to satisfy White House demands for more arrests while telling officers to use more restraint with their potent new tools. I CE started deploying license-plate readers nearly a decade ago. The technology was primarily reserved for criminal-investigation teams performing tasks such as tracking suspected drug smugglers. Law-enforcement agencies have generally found broad public support for the use of surveillance technologies when they’re used to catch dangerous criminals. Concerns about privacy and mass surveillance tend to arise when the government uses the technology for nonviolent offenses such as immigration violations. DHS’s civil-rights and civil-liberties officers have tried to limit the use of these tools by warning about the risk of privacy violations. According to a “Privacy Impact Assessment” published by the department in 2022, the use of plate readers is prohibited for “ad hoc” queries and to initiate traffic stops solely on the basis of a search result. The assessment said that ICE must limit use of the plate readers to officers with appropriate training, and require them to state a justification when using the technology. ICE is also required to maintain logs that are subject to quarterly internal audits. During the Biden administration, officers had to get supervisory approval to use the plate readers, a veteran ICE official told me, and officers were not authorized to do vehicle stops “except under very limited circumstances that would have necessitated that they KNEW who was in the car,” the official said. (This official, like others I spoke with, did so on the condition of anonymity because they’re not authorized to talk with reporters.) After immigration-enforcement officers shot and killed two U.S. citizens during the ICE crackdown in Minneapolis in January, the White House asked its “border czar,” Tom Homan, to calm tensions and shift tactics. Homan, who worked for many years at ICE, said officers would return to the “targeted enforcement” approach that the agency has traditionally employed. In practice, that meant fewer raids on Home Depot parking lots and more traffic stops. The plate readers helped ICE ramp up everywhere, but less visibly, one vehicle at a time. ICE did not respond to my questions about the expanded use of the automated plate readers. But Trump-administration officials have repeatedly said they have a duty to intensify immigration enforcement because the Biden administration allowed dangerous migrants to enter the United States en masse without proper screening. [ Read: ICE after the blowout ] Over the past several months, ICE has been piloting a new license-plate-reader mobile app that syncs with the agency’s databases, including its powerful new mapping tool, ELITE (Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement), which was developed by Palantir, the technology company. ICE officials I’ve spoken with say that ELITE has the ability to synthesize many of the databases they used to check one by one, potentially allowing them to quickly see phone numbers and addresses, motor-vehicle records, federal immigration files, Medicaid data, criminal records, and biometric information. Officers can simply point their phone at a license plate and pull up an individual’s case file and photo in a way that one ICE official likened to looking at a baseball card. A positive match in the ELITE system remains in the officers’ user history for 30 days, and searches that do not result in a match are deleted within 72 hours. Senior ICE leaders have been taking steps to rein in the use of the plate readers, perhaps in anticipation of increased oversight from incoming Democratic majorities in Congress. The agency has been developing new operation procedures to prohibit officers from using the plate readers to go “fishing” for targets at random, the way D.F. and L.G. used the devices, three ICE officials told me. Officers will likely be instructed to use the plate readers only as verification tools for subjects they’re already pursuing. But those guidelines have not been finalized or distributed. I CE remains under daily pressure from White House officials—especially Stephen Miller, the new chief of staff —to capture and deport as many people as possible, despite the administration’s claims that it is focused on “the worst of the worst.” The push to maximize arrests has resulted in a workplace culture in which officers are more likely to get in trouble for not taking action than they are for acting too aggressively, veteran officials have told me. ICE deported more than 483,000 people during the 2026 fiscal year, which ended September 30, the Department of Homeland Security announced this month. That is the highest one-year total ever, although it is still short of the administration’s goal of 1 million deportations a year. The ICE officials I spoke with said that arrests remain near record levels, at about 50,000 a month, and deportations are exceeding 42,000 a month. Traffic stops are essential to ICE’s arrest goals as the agency relies less on the tactic known as “knock and talk,” in which officers arrive at a subject’s residence and try to convince the person to open the door. ICE officers generally cannot force their way into a home without a warrant signed by a judge, and advocacy organizations have spread the word not to open doors for ICE, no matter how persuasive officers may be. Vehicles do not offer individuals the same constitutional privacy protections as homes do—which is one reason for the proliferation of videos showing ICE officers smashing car windows of drivers who disobey orders. Even in instances when ICE knows the address of a person they’re seeking to arrest, officers now typically wait until the person is in their car before attempting to apprehend them. [ Read: ICE has quietly changed its deadly-force rule ] The license-plate readers also help shield the agency from accusations of racial profiling. To initiate a vehicle stop, ICE officers must be able to articulate a “reasonable suspicion” that the individual is unlawfully present in the country. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a September 2025 opinion supporting the ability of federal agents and officers to use factors such as language and ethnic appearance when establishing reasonable suspicion, and such street-level checks are now known colloquially now as “ Kavanaugh stops .” When officers use plate readers, they’re leaving it to the technology to determine whom to pull over and check. ELITE creates neighborhood heat maps that show officers where they have the best chances of finding immigrants with deportation orders or criminal records, and others potentially subject to ICE arrest. ICE officers face a low risk of disciplinary action for initiating a stop on the basis of a license-plate-reader hit if they’re in a target-rich neighborhood that has a high percentage of immigrants subject to arrest, current and former ICE officials told me. They were skeptical that new guidelines on the use of the readers would curb their indiscriminate use, because of that low risk of disciplinary action. One former DHS official who worked on privacy issues likened the license-plate readers to a digital version of “stop-and-frisk,” allowing officers to go to immigrant neighborhoods and run checks on drivers who don’t appear white. Peter Mina, a former ICE attorney who was the deputy officer of the DHS Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, told me that the office’s oversight role has been weakened since President Trump returned for a second term. Working through the constitutional considerations involved in the use of new technologies such as automated plate readers is “the whole point of having a civil-rights office,” Mina said, and the technology “creates the potential for rampant civil-rights and civil-liberties abuses.” “I can’t imagine that all of a sudden someone in the chain of command is going to start monitoring and disciplining people, or counseling them, because they are indiscriminately using license-plate readers,” Mina said. “Because they’re probably feeling the same pressure to produce.” T he most extensive AI-powered plate-reader network in the United States is operated by Flock Safety, a company that has tried to cultivate a reputation for providing a neutral crime-fighting tool by avoiding controversial clients, including ICE. But lawmakers and privacy advocates have alleged that Flock cameras are being used by police agencies trying to investigate abortions as well as by ICE officers looking for immigrants—claims that the company denies. Flock is already facing a backlash in some cities and states, including Texas, where Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa ran a campaign ad showing her as a rifle-toting video-game character shooting down the cameras. The state has installed more than 10,000 plate readers linked to the Flock database, which is designed to provide law-enforcement officers with real-time location data on subjects they’re pursuing. Courtney Terlecki, a spokesperson for Flock, wrote to me that the company “is the only major license plate reader provider without a contract with the Department of Homeland Security.” Terlecki said the company provides customers with filters to block searches related to immigration enforcement, and every search must include a specified offense type and is recorded in an audit log. Critics of the surveillance technology say that ICE has found an easy work-around. Chad Marlow, a senior policy counsel at the ACLU, told me the group obtained records showing thousands of instances in which ICE officers had asked local and state police agencies to run searches of Flock data on their behalf. ICE says it has more than 2,600 agreements with state and local jurisdictions under the agency’s 287(g) program, up from 135 when Trump took office last year. Those partnerships are concentrated in Texas, Florida, and other southern states. According to Marlow, state and local police departments that partner with ICE have learned to avoid including terms such as immigration in their search logs. “We have seen searches where the ‘reason for the investigation’ put in was investigation , or hehehe , or LOL ,” Marlow told me. “There are no actual speed bumps within the system.” Communities had previously accepted the widespread deployment of plate-reader cameras on the premise of improved public safety, not civil immigration enforcement, Marlow added. Terlecki said that Flock customers “own their data and retain full control over it, including whether and with whom it is shared.” Last month, nearly three dozen lawmakers sent a letter to ICE Acting Director David Venturella objecting to what they called “side-door” access to the national network of Flock plate readers. The lawmakers said, “Chilling, unrestrained surveillance obtained without judicial authorization, contractual safeguards, or public transparency, represents far more than a procedural lapse—it represents the quiet expansion of a federal surveillance system operating out of sight and beyond any meaningful public oversight.” [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] The lawmakers told ICE they wanted a detailed breakdown by November 20 indicating how many times immigration officers had accessed Flock databases, how the data were used, and what other automated-plate-reader systems ICE is using. Representative Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, has proposed legislation to curb ICE’s use of facial-recognition software and other AI-powered apps. And he has pledged to conduct aggressive oversight of ICE when the Democratic majority takes control of Congress in January. His committee and others will be busy. Democrats have said they plan to investigate fatal shootings involving ICE officers conducting traffic stops, as well as the agency’s hiring surge last spring, its spending on detention centers and deportation flights, and allegations of inhumane conditions inside ICE facilities. With so much to choose from, it’s difficult to predict where license-plate readers may rank on their priority list.

items.title: Capitalising on Middle East conflict
items.description: Rarely does a government in Pakistan respond swiftly and purposefully to a crisis by bringing public and private stakeholders together, building consensus and implementing corrective measures. The US-Iran conflict presented such an opportunity, forcing Pakistan to protect its maritime supply chains while opening new possibilities for its ports and shipping industry. The prime minister constituted two committees to address the emerging challenges. This article focuses on the committee headed by Federal Minister for Maritime Affairs Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry, of which the writer was a member. Its mandate is to protect maritime trade flows and energy supplies while identifying opportunities arising from disruptions to regional shipping. The committee met regularly, sometimes daily, to address operational bottlenecks and develop a coordinated response. It helped maintain oil supplies and secure some liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes from Qatar despite force majeure following attacks on its production facilities and disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. One of its earliest initiatives followed an approach by the Pakistan Ship’s Agents Association (PSAA), which pointed out that disruption at major regional transshipment hubs offered Pakistan an opportunity to attract cargo previously routed through competing ports. Despite having a transshipment policy for more than two decades, Pakistan had failed to attract significant business because of restrictive customs procedures and uncompetitive port charges. US-Iran conflict is pushing Pakistan to protect its maritime supply chains and opening new possibilities for its ports and shipping industry The committee engaged customs authorities to remove these impediments. Rules were amended to allow transshipment cargo to be stored at off-dock terminals, easing pressure on congested on-dock facilities. The requirement for mandatory scanning of all containers moving to off-dock terminals was also replaced with a risk-based non-intrusive inspection system. Customs procedures were further revised to accommodate non-containerised break-bulk and roll-on/roll-off cargo. New feeder shipping services to Gulf and Red Sea ports were also encouraged to maintain outlets for Pakistani imports and exports amid disruption to established shipping routes. Another significant achievement came on July 29, when the Joint War Committee of Lloyd’s London formally stated that war-risk insurance premiums for vessels calling at Pakistani ports would no longer be automatically triggered by their classification under listed areas. This is expected to reduce shipping costs and improve the commercial attractiveness of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar, removing a reputational disadvantage that had affected Pakistan’s ports for more than a decade. The committee also addressed the longstanding problem of auctioned containers occupying valuable port space. Customs authorities allowed these containers to be shifted to licensed off-dock facilities, freeing terminal capacity, facilitating faster cargo handling and enabling shipping lines to redeploy their containers for fresh business. Another breakthrough was permission for less-than-container-load (LCL) transshipment. This involves importing smaller consignments, consolidating or deconsolidating cargo, undertaking value addition and re-exporting it. Pakistan has long sought to develop this business along the lines of Jebel Ali. One major US-based shipping company has already selected Pakistan over India for its LCL transshipment operations. Gwadar Port also witnessed a notable increase in activity, receiving more than a dozen vessels carrying around 200,000 tonnes of transshipment cargo, including steel plates, machinery and fertiliser, within three months. This exceeded the vessel and cargo activity recorded during the preceding three years. Five additional vessels conducted anchorage operations. To improve competitiveness, reduced port and terminal tariffs were introduced for transshipment cargo, with concessions linked to the proportion of such cargo handled. A Far Eastern shipping company has consequently expressed interest in shifting its transshipment operations from India’s Mundra Port to Karachi. The committee also took up complaints about excessive and retrospective war-risk and emergency conflict surcharges imposed by shipping companies, including on cargo that had sailed before the conflict began. Customs authorities directed shipping lines and their agents to ensure transparency, disclose charges in advance and refrain from unjustified retrospective levies. A mechanism was established for affected importers and exporters to submit documentary evidence for scrutiny. Importantly, revised customs procedures will allow consignees to choose between on-dock and off-dock terminals for cargo clearance. This will enable cargo to be moved directly to off-dock facilities, where shipping containers can be emptied and returned promptly, reducing detention and demurrage costs while improving port turnaround times. The committee’s recommendations were subsequently submitted to the prime minister, who constituted the National Coordination and Management Council to coordinate decisions concerning the economic, trade and energy consequences of the Middle East conflict. The next phase offers further opportunities. The Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Port Qasim Authority are working on a proposed automobile import and re-export zone where used vehicles could be imported, refurbished and exported. Much of this business is currently conducted in Dubai and Sharjah, often by Pakistani operators. A proposed energy city at Port Qasim or another suitable location could also provide strategic petroleum storage outside the Strait of Hormuz. International energy companies have reportedly expressed interest. The potential economic gains extend beyond port revenues to shipping, logistics, storage, transportation and employment. Each transshipment container handled in Pakistan could generate an estimated $150 in associated economic activity. An additional throughput of 500,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) is achievable within one to three years, rising to one million within five years. The crisis has demonstrated that trade facilitation is essential to Pakistan’s economic competitiveness. A trade facilitation board is expected to examine remaining bottlenecks in cargo clearance and logistics costs. Sustaining these gains, however, will require consistent policies, institutional coordination and a lasting commitment to removing regulatory friction. The writer is chairman Pakistan Ship’s Agents Association and former board member of KPT, PQA and GPIA Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 23rd, 2026

items.title: Integrate legal education into teacher training
items.description: Teaching is undoubtedly one of the few professions where the actions of an individual can have lifelong consequences for others. Beyond imparting knowledge, teachers are entrusted with the responsibility of shaping character, instilling discipline and protecting the welfare of learners. But how adequately are we preparing our teachers to appreciate the legal consequences of their actions and decisions in the classroom? This is a question worth considering as Ghana continues to pursue reforms aimed at improving teacher professionalism and the quality of education. Over the years, considerable attention has been given to strengthening teachers’ pedagogical competencies, subject knowledge, assessment practices and classroom management skills. However, one important area that deserves equal attention is legal education. I believe the time has come for Ghana to consider introducing basic legal education into the teacher education curriculum, particularly at the pre-service level. Teacher education reforms Ghana’s teacher education sector has witnessed significant reforms over the past decade, particularly following the introduction of the four-year Bachelor of Education programme in 2018. The National Teacher Education Curriculum Framework (NTECF) and the National Teachers’ Standards (NTS) have provided important directions for preparing teachers who are professionally competent and responsive to the changing demands of education. These reforms are commendable. Nevertheless, as the teaching profession evolves, so must the competencies expected of those entering it. Today, teachers operate in an increasingly complex environment where their decisions may have legal implications beyond the administrative sanctions traditionally associated with professional misconduct. Issues involving corporal punishment, sexual harassment, discrimination, negligence, child protection and the inappropriate use of learners’ personal information have become important concerns within our educational institutions. Unfortunately, some teachers may not fully appreciate that actions considered disciplinary measures or ordinary classroom practices could potentially expose them to civil or criminal liability. Should we wait until teachers find themselves facing legal proceedings before educating them about their legal responsibilities? Understanding legal consequences The essence of introducing legal education into teacher training is not to produce lawyers in our classrooms. Rather, it is to equip prospective teachers with fundamental knowledge of the laws governing their profession and the rights of learners. Consider a teacher who physically assaults a learner under the guise of maintaining discipline. Beyond violating professional standards, such conduct may constitute a criminal offence or expose the teacher to civil action. Similarly, a teacher who engages in an inappropriate relationship with a learner may face serious legal consequences, particularly where the conduct involves a child. There are also situations where teachers disclose confidential information about learners, discriminate against pupils with disabilities or fail to exercise reasonable care during school activities. These examples demonstrate why professional ethics alone, although essential, may not sufficiently prepare teachers to understand the legal implications of their conduct. A basic understanding of Ghana’s Children’s Act, 1998 (Act 560), the Education Regulatory Bodies Act, 2020 (Act 1023), the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), and relevant provisions of the 1992 Constitution could provide a useful foundation. Importantly, teachers must understand that ignorance of the law does not ordinarily excuse unlawful conduct. Teachers as agents of change Beyond protecting teachers from avoidable legal difficulties, legal education has broader implications for national development. Teachers are among the most influential agents of social change, particularly in communities where schools remain important centres for promoting citizenship, discipline and responsible behaviour. A teacher who understands fundamental human rights, child protection laws and civic responsibilities is better positioned to nurture learners who respect the rights of others. Such knowledge can also empower teachers to identify and appropriately report cases of child abuse, exploitation and other violations affecting learners. In this regard, legal education should not merely emphasise punishment and legal consequences. It must equally promote justice, fairness, accountability and respect for human dignity. After all, how can teachers effectively nurture responsible citizens when they themselves have limited appreciation of the legal principles underpinning responsible citizenship? Integrating legal education Introducing legal education should not necessarily require an extensive restructuring of the existing teacher education curriculum. The Ministry of Education, through the relevant regulatory institutions, could initiate stakeholder consultations to explore the development of a foundational course in Education Law and Professional Responsibilities. Such a course could cover the legal framework governing education in Ghana, children’s rights, teachers’ rights and responsibilities, professional negligence, workplace misconduct, safeguarding and emerging legal issues associated with technology. Practical case studies drawn from Ghanaian educational settings should constitute an important component of the course. This would enable student teachers to examine real-life situations, appreciate the consequences of particular decisions and develop appropriate professional responses. The Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), National Teaching Council (NTC), mentoring universities and colleges of education could collaborate with law faculties and legal practitioners to develop suitable course content. Additionally, aspects of legal education could be incorporated into continuing professional development programmes for teachers already serving in our schools. The way forward As Ghana seeks to strengthen the teaching profession, we must recognise that professional competence extends beyond the ability to deliver lessons effectively. Teachers must also understand the legal boundaries within which they exercise their professional authority. I am convinced that introducing basic legal education into our teacher education curriculum will strengthen professionalism, safeguard learners and minimise avoidable legal challenges confronting teachers. It will also contribute to producing educators who are not only academically and pedagogically competent but legally informed and socially responsible. Ultimately, the objective should be to prepare teachers who understand not only how to teach, but also the legal consequences of how they act. The time to begin this conversation is now.
